Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed that it has fallen significantly since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, given (1) expectations of a decline in the national savings rate due to an increase in the fiscal deficit, and (2) the possibility that corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment of capital expenditures could lead to an increase in investment rates, the U.S. R* may face upward pressure in the future. An increase in R*, combined with expectations of an increase in term premiums due to the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalization, could signal that long-term interest rates will rise, thereby putting pressure on asset market valuations. Chart 2.6: U.S. R* estimated by the Laubach-Williams model. Third, the strengthening of growth momentum in the eurozone and Japan has led markets to expect that their central banks may reduce monetary easing measures. If this happens, it could signal a simultaneous tightening of global monetary conditions. In the eurozone, member economies have experienced a broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economy has also recovered at an accelerated pace, with real GDP recording positive growth for the eighth consecutive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continue to signal that they will maintain accommodative monetary policies in the face of weak inflation, the brightening economic growth outlook in Europe and Japan (and the continued tightening of Japan's labor market) has led some market participants to predict that they will further reduce their quantitative easing programs in the near future. Chart 2.7: Real GDP of selected eurozone member countries. Policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent recovery in global economic growth and trade. The U.S. government appears to be more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, as evidenced by the imposition of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines announced in January 2018, and the announcement of import tariffs on steel and aluminum in early March, raising concerns that its trading partners may respond with retaliatory measures. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom is currently negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements with other EU countries, a process that involves many uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade frictions, they could hinder global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions (such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East, and the risk of terrorist attacks) could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum further strengthened in the second half of 2017, ending the year with a strong performance. Actual growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. Foreign trade remained the main driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided stable support (Chart 2.8). The accelerated recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted exports in the region. Chart 2.8: East Asia: Domestic demand and exports. Inflationary pressures have remained weak so far. In the second half of 2017, overall inflation in East Asia eased, driven by lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained at a low level in many economies due to slow wage growth. Chart 2.9: East Asia: Overall and core consumer price inflation rates. *Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and individual central banks. The economic upturn was accompanied by substantial capital inflows, causing financial asset prices to rise significantly in 2017 and early 2018 (Chart 2.10, blue and pink bars). The volume of capital inflows to the region rebounded significantly in 2017, with total net inflows of portfolio investment reaching a new high since 2010. Valuations of various types of financial assets in the region also rose along with market gains. In fact, credit risk premiums in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, and benchmark stock indices across the region rose across the board. Currencies in the region generally appreciated against the U.S. dollar.

Amid robust domestic demand and an improvement in export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained strong growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. The outlook for the local economy continues to be subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, fluctuations in global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, while domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy sustained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% recorded in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained one of the key drivers of GDP growth. The robust consumption growth was supported by favorable employment and income conditions, continued optimism among consumers, and a positive wealth effect from rising asset prices. Although property and construction activities weakened, an increase in business capital spending led to a significant rise in overall investment expenditure in the final quarter, following three quarters of broadly stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, net exports of goods continued to weigh on GDP growth as import growth outpaced export growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure components; Chart 3.2: Real imports and exports. The sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by about 0.7% to over 3.85 million during the period, with the most significant increases recorded in the construction sector, the financial and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labor productivity showed further signs of improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. Externally, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improved global economic growth outlook and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly due to favorable labor market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Special Topic 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage payment burdens on private consumption. As for domestic fixed capital formation, property and construction activities should grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued rollout of infrastructure projects. Although an improved economic environment will stimulate business capital spending, the potential for interest rate hikes could have an adverse effect. The Government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2018 will be between 3% and 4%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth prospects remain subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment discussed in previous chapters, the performance of the Mainland Chinese economy amid tighter financial conditions, and developments in local asset markets. Domestic inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although there were signs of a slight pickup in month-on-month inflation momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum on a three-month annualized basis, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Both tradable goods and services prices increased. The rebound in newly signed private residential rents since mid-2016 may also have contributed to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labor cost pressures remained moderate over the past few quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3: Different indicators of consumer price inflation; Chart 3.4: CCPI rent component and market rents; Chart 3.5: Unit labor cost and per capita wages. Given that global inflation remains subdued and domestic cost increases are stable, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to stay moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from the eight-year low of 1.7% recorded in 2017. For example, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effect from growth in newly signed private residential rents. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2018 is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government's forecast for underlying inflation is 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. Externally, any larger-than-expected increase in global inflation or commodity prices could boost domestic inflation momentum. Domestically, the labor market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, the first time it has been below 3% in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant tightening of the labor market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6: Unemployment rate. Following the 2008 global financial crisis, interest rates remained low and Hong Kong households' mortgage debt increased. As the normalization of US dollar interest rates progresses, Hong Kong dollar rates will eventually follow suit and rise, leading to a corresponding increase in future household mortgage payment burdens, which will weigh on household consumption. This special topic therefore examines the impact of higher mortgage payment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage payment burden refers to the proportion of income accounted for by mortgage debt-servicing payments (i.e., interest payments plus loan principal repayments). Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage payment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices as mentioned in general economic theory, an interest rate shock will also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments and, consequently, households' disposable income when a mortgage payment burden exists. This effect will be amplified as outstanding mortgage loan balances increase. Furthermore, loan principal repayments vary with changes in outstanding mortgage loan balances, which will also affect private consumption by altering households' disposable income. Chart B3.1: Determinants of private consumption. To measure the impact of mortgage payment burden on private consumption, we estimated the ratio of outstanding mortgage payments to income (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike existing mortgage payment burden indicators that apply only to newly originated mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt held by households, which is more closely related to total private consumption. We largely followed the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, employing a standard formula for fixed installment payments to measure the OMDSR: where Dt represents outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt represents total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st represent the average interest rate and maturity period of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure mortgage payment burden across the entire household sector, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used payment burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows estimates of the OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on quinquennial population censuses. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997 and the substantial decline in mortgage interest rates during the same period. Despite a sharp rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, owing to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA) macroprudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the extension of loan maturities for newly originated mortgages reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2: OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income. We also compared the OMDSR with banks' loan-to-income (LTI) ratio, which represents the actual debt-servicing-to-income ratio of new mortgage applicants at banks. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' LTI ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only newly originated mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since existing mortgages were taken out when property prices were lower, their payments are correspondingly lower than those of newly originated mortgages. Therefore, an outstanding mortgage payment burden indicator that covers both existing and newly originated mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) will be lower than an indicator that covers only newly originated mortgages (i.e., banks' LTI ratio). Additionally, banks' LTI ratio is higher because banks, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements, include repayments of non-mortgage loans when calculating the LTI ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' LTI ratio remained stable, mainly due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential regulations on mortgage lending, which set a cap on banks' LTI ratio; this measure also helped to stabilize the OMDSR. Chart B3.3: OMDSR and banks' LTI ratio for newly originated mortgages. Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used payment burden indicators, but it has greater timeliness and can reflect the burden of total outstanding mortgage debt, rather than just newly originated mortgage debt. We therefore believe that using the OMDSR can assess the impact of mortgage payment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage payment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model (ECM) following the methodology of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we identified real income (proxied by median household income deflated by the CCPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, both deflated by the CCPI), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has weakened, but the local interbank market continues to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to grow, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalization process continues, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment shifts sharply, capital flow volatility could increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot rate briefly strengthened from September to November 2017, remaining near 7.80. This was mainly due to increased funding demand from new equity offerings and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management toward month-end and year-end, which tightened liquidity conditions, thereby slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and prompting an increase in short-covering of Hong Kong dollar positions. As the tightness in Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased and US dollar commercial demand rose toward year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot rate weakened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the convertibility guarantee was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2: Capital flow indicator. The Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017 but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This movement is broadly consistent with the US dollar's performance against most major currencies. Given that the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners is small and has limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate index continued to move closely in line with the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3: Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Non-resident securities investment recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics show that both local and non-resident equity securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved regional economic prospects and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-resident debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows in local residents' debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that, owing to market optimism about economic prospects and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, the survey data indicated that, despite adjustments in global financial markets, equity investment continued to record inflows, while bond investment recorded slight outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4: Market survey of capital flows related to equities and bonds. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalization process continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, potentially leading to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility that the Hong Kong dollar weak-side convertibility guarantee will be triggered cannot be ruled out. This is a normal process under the linked exchange rate system. At the same time, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalization remains uncertain and global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are subject to rapid change, volatility in Hong Kong dollar capital flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to ensure the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to the fullest extent under the currency board mechanism. Despite the US Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and more recently. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base rose further by 1.4%, mainly due to growth in liabilities certificates issued for the issue of banknotes (Chart 4.5). Since the convertibility guarantee was not triggered, the aggregate balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund bills and notes remained essentially unchanged in the second half of the year, standing at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this, the aggregate balance declined, while outstanding Exchange Fund bills and notes increased accordingly. This was due to the issuance of additional Exchange Fund bills (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' substantial demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite adjustments in the stock market, the monetary base remained stable. Chart 4.5: Components of the monetary base. Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar money supply continued to grow in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Growth in Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose modestly by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Of these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. Corresponding asset analysis shows that Hong Kong dollar M3 growth was supported by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), but was offset by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6: Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its corresponding assets. On the other hand, foreign currency deposits showed mixed performance. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after declining for over two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by a recent recovery in renminbi deposits. Owing to slower growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits, total deposits of authorized institutions increased only slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For the full year of 2017, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7: Deposit growth. From September to December 2017, increased funding demand from new equity offerings and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management toward month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points, respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (based on monthly averages). The negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates for tenors from 1 month to 3 months also narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8: Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly mirroring the movement of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half of the year, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds increased by a smaller 33 basis points to 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9: Government bond yields; composite interest rate and average new mortgage lending rate. Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates fell in early January. Thereafter, despite adjustments in global and local equity markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained broadly stable. The overnight and 3-month HIBOR stood at 0.43% and 1.08%, respectively, at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose alongside the increase in HIBOR, banks' funding costs generally remained low, given the still substantial deposit base. Despite intense competition in mortgage lending, banks' average new mortgage lending rate rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs, rose briefly in October due to increased funding demand from new equity offerings, but remained soft for most of the second half, ending at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalization process continues and other major economies may initiate interest rate normalization, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase capital flow volatility. However, the substantial Hong Kong dollar monetary base can serve as a buffer, helping to moderate any excessive rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and the availability of discount window facilities will help curb excessive volatility in interbank rates. Bank credit grew strongly in 2017 as a whole. The loan growth rate reached 10.2% in the first half, then slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, growth in both loans used in Hong Kong and those used outside Hong Kong slowed. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly at 9.5% in the second half, supported by a favorable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, while foreign currency loans rose only slightly by 0.1%. Of these, US dollar loan growth slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. For the full year of 2017, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10: Loan growth. Growth in loans used in Hong Kong (including trade finance) fell from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with performance varying across major industries (Chart 4.11). Loan growth in the construction sector and for property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities required banks to strengthen risk management of loans to property developers from June 2017 onward. Despite further improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade finance and loans to the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail sectors fell. By contrast, loans to finance- and financial-related enterprises continued to grow strongly, reflecting, to some extent, the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11: Local loan growth by selected industries. Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with an increase of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, private loans (including credit card advances and other private-purpose loans) accelerated further, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in private loans was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management clients using financial assets as collateral. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the continued increase in client assets managed by banks. The risk associated with such collateralized loans remains within manageable levels. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks on private loan risk management in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the loan-to-value ratios of newly approved mortgages fell, and residential mortgage loan growth slowed slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Retail banking profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016, primarily benefiting from growth in net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions remained robust. After strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit expansion slowed in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR), retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs stayed low, owing to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should remain vigilant about the risks of rising interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows resulting from the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and high household debt levels, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates increase more than expected. To enhance banks' resilience to systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, overall pre-tax operating profits of retail banks grew by 13.6% year-on-year. This was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets (ROA) of retail banks fell slightly to 1.15% in the second half of 2017, from 1.17% in the first half. Nevertheless, the ROA in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2017, overall pre-tax operating profits of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while ROA rose to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Chart 5.1: Retail banking profitability. The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017, from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Evidence suggests that the improvement in NIMs was consistent with an increase in the average spread for Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2: Net interest margin of retail banks; Chart 5.3: Average spread of Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans. Since September 2017, HIBOR has risen across all tenors, driven mainly by initial public offering (IPO)-related activities, banks' funding needs towards the year-end, and expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, the 3-month HIBOR reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, though it remained low by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, HIBOR appears to have stabilised as banks' year-end funding needs eased. Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs have remained stable. This is mainly because retail deposit rates stayed low during the review period. As a result, the composite rate, which reflects the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, remained low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before rising slightly to 0.38% at the end of December (the green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was observed for the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks' average non-deposit market funding costs for Hong Kong dollar and US dollar rose by 35 basis points, while average deposit funding costs increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4: Interest rates; Chart 5.5: Funding costs and tenors for Hong Kong dollar and US dollar of licensed banks. The increase in HIBOR has outpaced the rise in the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the interest rate spreads on banks' assets that are benchmarked to HIBOR. However, this improvement could be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market data show that some banks have narrowed the margin between their mortgage rates and the benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater pressure from rising funding costs. Given the fierce competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks' net interest margins. The overall capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions remains well above international minimum standards, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector maintains strong capital buffers. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.6: Capital of locally incorporated authorised institutions. The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper to seek views on the rules to be made under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance to implement loss-absorbing capacity (LAC) requirements for authorised institutions. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorised institutions helps reduce the likelihood of a financial crisis, thereby benefiting society, it inevitably entails costs. Special Topic 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of LAC requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing LAC requirements will generate net benefits for the Hong Kong economy. In terms of the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions rose to 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2017, from 144.2% in the second quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) for Category 2 institutions fell slightly to 49.4% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 49.7% in the second quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorised institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks that could result from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), another Basel III liquidity standard, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. This requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- and long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain an NSFR of at least 100% at all times. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorised institutions, reflecting the banking system's stable funding structure. At the end of December 2017, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorised institutions was largely unchanged from six months earlier, remaining at 56.2% (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8: Liability structure of all authorised institutions. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions rose to 82.7% at the end of December 2017, from 77.1% at the end of June (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at the end of December 2017 from 65.5% at the end of June, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose to 73.0% from 71.4% six months earlier. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. Chart 5.9: Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions. Interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. We estimate that, under a shock scenario of a 200 basis point increase in interest rates across the board, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate position of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 3.45% of their total capital base as of the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the US Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and commence balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10: Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks. In the second half of 2017, under a moderate but still favourable economic environment, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorised institutions slowed to 5.3%, from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of slower growth, total loans grew robustly by 16.1% for the full year of 2017. Asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the total specific classification ratio and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans of all authorised institutions fell to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the total specific classification ratio and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans also fell to 0.54% and 0.40% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in recent years of loans used outside Hong Kong, banks' asset quality may be more sensitive to external conditions, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11: Asset quality of retail banks. As banks have become more optimistic about recent credit growth, strong credit expansion is expected to continue. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Survey" in December 2017 showed that 29% of the surveyed authorised institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk for personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio for newly approved mortgages fell further to 48.8% in the fourth quarter of 2017, from 50.1% in the second quarter (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio is well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA implemented the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures in September 2009.

The global economy continued to grow, but its momentum weakened amid heightened uncertainty stemming from persistent trade frictions, tighter financial conditions, and other special and cyclical headwinds. The US Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and that "patience" was required, leading investors to rule out the possibility of further interest rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to upcoming data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. In Hong Kong, despite the Hong Kong dollar triggering the weak-side convertibility undertaking in March, trading of the currency remained smooth and orderly. In the second half of 2018, overall loan growth slowed slightly, reflecting reduced credit demand amid headwinds such as the ongoing US-China trade conflict and a slowdown in global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes falling significantly and property prices declining, before showing signs of stabilization in early 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s banking sector faces multiple challenges due to increased uncertainty in the external environment. If this uncertainty intensifies and persists over the long term, it could significantly dampen business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potential deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum slowed in other regions. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major eurozone countries experienced slower growth and low inflation. A slowdown in global trade and a sharp decline in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds for emerging market economies. Given the slowdown in global growth, the International Monetary Fund revised its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 downward by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, compared to its October 2018 projections. Amid dimming growth prospects and escalating trade frictions, global equity markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, raising market concerns about an impending recession in the United States. However, the US economy’s fundamentals remain strong, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term is low. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainty. In the United States, while moderate inflation provides the Federal Reserve with room to pause interest rate hikes, the Fed’s data-dependent policy stance suggests that financial markets may become more sensitive to upcoming data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the United States and China, as well as between the United States and the European Union, remain uncertain. In the United Kingdom, it remains unclear whether a solution to avoid a "hard Brexit" can be achieved. In East Asia, financial markets have stabilized due to a slowdown in the US dollar’s appreciation and market expectations that the Federal Reserve will pause interest rate hikes, but a deterioration in the external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. In fact, weaker global trade growth has already dampened economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures have eased. Although this shift may alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks in balancing growth support and inflation control, financial imbalances, such as high private-sector leverage in some countries in the region, remain severe. As detailed in Special Feature 1 (page 16), another challenge facing the East Asian region is that unexpected changes in the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy could have spillover effects on sovereign bond markets in emerging market economies, including those in East Asia. In mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 due to increased external uncertainty and a slight slowdown in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain as US-China trade negotiations have yet to reach a conclusion. A significant contraction in shadow financing activities has increased financing difficulties for private enterprises, especially small companies, over the past few quarters, and weakening economic confidence may also put pressure on business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers must continue to strike a balance between stabilizing the economy and mitigating potential systemic risks by adopting accommodative yet targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement reductions. At the same time, authorities are implementing more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among companies of different ownership types, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%, down from around 6.5% in 2018. In 2018, risk aversion dominated mainland China’s financial markets. Bank asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while leverage levels among listed non-financial companies rose modestly. However, bank loan loss provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, and their exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments helped protect the banking system from potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that leverage levels among listed companies in overcapacity industries—one of the main sources of credit risk for banks—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Special Feature 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors driving the recent improvement in the performance of overcapacity industries. Compared to the first half of 2018, economic activity in Hong Kong weakened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stalled, and year-on-year growth slowed, causing full-year economic growth to decelerate from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to the direct or indirect impact of the US-China trade conflict on consumption and exports. The slowdown in private consumption may reflect increased economic uncertainty and the wealth-dampening effect of adjustments in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong’s merchandise export performance also deteriorated, particularly after the United States and China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Special Feature 3 examines in greater detail the impact of the US-China trade conflict on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and explores the short-term outlook and associated risks. Economic growth is expected to slow further in 2019, primarily due to a slowdown in global economic growth. Under the combined influence of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue supporting economic growth, given low unemployment and rising household incomes, but the outlook for overall investment spending may become more uncertain. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2019 will be between 2% and 3%, while the latest growth forecasts from private-sector analysts average 2.3%. These forecasts are subject to the various uncertainties and risks outlined above. Local inflation rose slightly in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The modest increase in inflation was partly driven by earlier growth in newly signed local private residential rents. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in more than two decades, there were signs of a slowdown in overall employment growth. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate as domestic economic growth momentum weakens in 2019. Following the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side convertibility undertaking was triggered again in March 2019, for a total of four times (as of March 19). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity conditions. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly due to the re-establishment of carry trade positions. Despite the weak-side convertibility undertaking being triggered again in March, trading of the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking, the aggregate balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared to June 2018, 3-month and 12-month HIBOR rose by about 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74%, respectively, in December (on a monthly average basis). Entering 2019, HIBOR generally fell due to a decline in seasonal demand. The composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banks, rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. Given the rise in funding costs, following the increase in the US federal funds rate target range at the end of September, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. At the end of January 2019, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.45%, following the increase in the best lending rate. Given the continued uncertainty surrounding US-China trade frictions and Brexit negotiations, capital flow volatility may intensify. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate arbitrage trading activities, leading to capital outflows. In this context, both capital outflows and the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking are normal operations under the linked exchange rate system. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have been under depreciation pressure due to market concerns about escalating US-China trade frictions. However, driven by optimism following the resumption of high-level trade talks between the United States and China, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilized in November. Although US-China trade frictions persist, they have not yet had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. The overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR in Hong Kong remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-time Gross Settlement System remained high and further increased to RMB 10.101 trillion in 2018. Despite concerns about US-China trade frictions, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to continue to expand, driven by the opening of mainland China’s capital account, the development of stock and bond connectivity, and regional economic cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives. The local stock market has experienced significant volatility over the past six months, resembling a roller coaster ride. At the beginning of the review period, the market experienced a sharp decline due to continued tightening of US monetary policy, significant differences between the United States and China in trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in mainland China. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance, while China took further measures to reduce its trade surplus with the United States and open its market to foreign investors during a trade war truce. Although the United States brought highly politicized legal charges against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides demonstrated a friendly attitude, indicating a determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local stock market rebounded sharply at the beginning of the year. However, the future remains highly uncertain as the two sides discuss the details of any agreement, and the developments surrounding the US federal government’s legal charges will further complicate the situation, particularly in the high-tech sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields fell, and performance improved toward the end of the year as market expectations for a slower pace of US monetary policy normalization increased. As a result, capital flows into bond funds reversed and increased slightly in the second half of the year. Issuance in Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi market rebounded significantly after three consecutive years of decline. However, as mainland Chinese companies continued to deleverage, total issuance remained lower than maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remains challenging, and its prospects depend on global economic developments, particularly those in mainland China.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but its momentum weakened amid a combination of special and cyclical headwinds, particularly in regions outside the United States. Given the dimmer growth outlook, the Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data dependent" and that "patience" would be required, while discontinuing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. Since the Fed's policy orientation is data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to upcoming data releases and may perceive monetary policy as more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainty surrounding global trade policies and escalating geopolitical risks could continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have largely stabilized since the end of 2018, owing to signs of a slowdown in the US interest rate hike cycle and a steadier US dollar. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown due to a deteriorating external environment, namely the unresolved US–China trade conflict and weaker growth in advanced economies. In mainland China, growth momentum further decelerated in the second half of 2018, and uncertainty regarding the growth outlook increased amid the US–China trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Consequently, policymakers have adopted additional targeted measures to stabilize the economy and support private and small businesses. In addressing these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to guard against systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to expand overall. However, while the US economy's performance remained broadly robust, some signs of slowdown emerged. There were also clear indications that growth momentum had weakened in regions outside the United States. Several country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a sharp rise in Italian government bond yields due to a fiscal standoff with the European Union, and social unrest in France—dampened economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). Moreover, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed a headwind to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). A sharp drop in oil prices in the fourth quarter also presented new challenges for emerging market economies that export commodities. Given the slowdown in growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage point to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1: Composite Purchasing Managers' Index for Selected Advanced Economies; Chart 2.2: Global Import Volumes and Industrial Production in Emerging Market Economies. In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent a significant correction, driven by slower global growth momentum, heightened uncertainty over trade policies, market concerns about the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and statements from the Federal Reserve indicating that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels unseen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to fear an impending US recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3: Spread between 10-Year and 3-Month US Treasury Yields and Probability of a US Recession. Nevertheless, the likelihood of a US recession in the near term remains very low. The US economy's fundamentals are still solid, particularly given a tight labor market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, making it less likely that the economy will overheat and compel the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy aggressively. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Federal Reserve officials began emphasizing in early January that monetary policy would be data dependent, noting that moderate inflationary pressures would allow them to exercise "patience" in determining future policy adjustments. Furthermore, following its January meeting, the US Federal Open Market Committee discontinued forward guidance on further interest rate hikes and announced that it "would consider changes in economic and financial conditions in adjusting any details of the balance sheet normalization process." This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4: S&P 500, MSCI World (ex-US) Index, and MSCI Emerging Markets Index. Despite the Federal Reserve's recent "dovish" signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains highly uncertain and will depend on inflation and other developments. Inflationary pressures have been moderate to date, giving the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary normalization. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that "patience can be exercised" (Chart 2.5). Additionally, as Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple downside risks, including slower growth outside the United States and uncertainty over trade policies. Given these developments, the Federal Reserve may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5: Market- and Survey-Based Measures of US Inflation Expectations. However, a tight labor market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically implies that future inflation could rise (Chart 2.6). Consequently, market expectations that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates in 2019 at all may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6: Average Hourly Earnings and Core Personal Consumption Expenditures Inflation; Chart 2.7: Probability (derived from futures markets) that the Federal Funds Target Range will remain unchanged in 2019 versus the probability of at least one rate hike. In summary, a prolonged pause in interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve is not a certainty. To minimize policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasized that its decisions will be data dependent as part of its risk management strategy. Accordingly, financial markets may become more sensitive to upcoming data releases, especially those that could prompt monetary policy tightening. Monetary policy outlooks for other major central banks are also uncertain. In the eurozone, the European Central Bank terminated its asset purchase program in December, while continuing to reinvest the full principal of securities maturing under the program, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its short-term growth assessment in January, describing the risks to the growth outlook as "skewed to the downside." The impact of the ECB's downward revision of its economic growth assessment on monetary policy remains to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary, given increased downside risks. However, further monetary easing may face significant obstacles, as its effectiveness is being questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment for an extended period are becoming more apparent; for example, regional banks' capital ratios have fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018, owing to persistently low profitability caused by low yields. Consequently, the Bank of Japan has very limited scope to adjust its monetary policy in the near term. In addition to uncertainty surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, the uncertain outcome of future trade negotiations and escalating geopolitical risks are two major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. The US government announced in early December that it would not increase tariffs on Chinese imports for 90 days, and extended this deadline again at the end of February; however, whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the United States and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. Given that the outcomes of these trade negotiations remain uncertain, they could continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the United States, partisan disagreements over border security funding led to a 35-day government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the shutdown's impact on economic growth should be short-lived, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives could lead to further policy impasses in the future. In the United Kingdom, risks related to Brexit and its spillover effects surged after Prime Minister Theresa May's Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and it remains uncertain whether a solution can be devised at the last minute to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit." Elsewhere, heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as renewed US sanctions on Iran, could also create uncertainty regarding oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets largely stabilized in the fourth quarter after fluctuating throughout the first three quarters of the year. The US dollar has steadied since October, and there are signs that the Federal Reserve will exercise patience regarding further interest rate hikes, easing pressure on East Asian economies from currency depreciation and capital outflows. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8: East Asia – Currency Index and Capital Flows. Despite the stabilization of financial markets, there are growing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. Weaker global trade momentum due to the US–China trade conflict has led to a decline in export growth, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of the year. Indeed, the new export orders component of the Purchasing Managers' Index for several regional economies (which reflects short-term external trade performance) has fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that short-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9: New Export Orders Index in the Markit Purchasing Managers' Index for East Asian Economies. Amid the environment of slowing growth, coupled with recent declines in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10: East Asia – Overall Inflation Rate and Oil Prices. Given that recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar have been relatively moderate, East Asian central banks have no urgent need to raise interest rates, which alleviates the policy dilemma of balancing the promotion of economic growth against the suppression of inflation and capital outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face challenges related to financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

Hong Kong's economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weaker export performance amid the US–China trade dispute. With global growth expected to moderate, real GDP growth in 2019 is also projected to slow. The city's growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the performance of the Mainland economy. Domestic inflation pressure in 2019 should remain moderate, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. Economic activity in Hong Kong weakened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the economy failed to sustain the strong momentum seen in the first half, with the quarter-on-quarter GDP growth rate turning slightly negative (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the fourth-quarter growth rate at 1.3%, below the trend rate, pulling down the full-year growth rate from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018.* Based on the expenditure-based and seasonally adjusted real GDP volume index. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure components. The weakening in economic activity was mainly due to a drag on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect impact of the US–China trade conflict. Private consumption growth slowed, possibly reflecting increased economic uncertainty and a wealth-dampening effect from adjustments in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Total investment spending declined significantly amid fragile business confidence. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after the United States and Mainland China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, the trade balance still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter, as imports contracted faster than exports. Special Topic 3 will examine Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance in greater detail and explore its short-term prospects and associated risks. Chart 3.2: Real imports and exports. As economic activity weakened, employment growth appeared to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, a slower pace than the 0.8% increase in the first half of the year. With weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly flat, showing no signs of significant improvement. Given the further slowdown in global economic growth, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. In the face of external challenges, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, although low unemployment and rising household incomes will continue to support private consumption, private consumption growth is expected to slow, partly affected by weaker consumer confidence and a wealth-dampening effect from earlier asset price adjustments. The outlook for fixed capital formation may become more uncertain. While building and construction activity is expected to grow steadily with increased housing supply, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment amid heightened economic uncertainty. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index continue to hover in contractionary territory, and the index's forward-looking gauge of economic growth points to a further slowdown in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2% to 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts from private-sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong's growth outlook is subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed in the previous two chapters. Although domestic inflation pressure has continued to build up in recent months, it remains moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018, respectively, higher than the 2.4% average increase in the first half of the year. The underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum and is measured on a three-month moving annualised basis, has also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight rise in inflation momentum was driven by increases in some service prices. Earlier increases in newly signed private residential rents and faster rises in dining-out prices continued to push up service inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressure has remained broadly moderate over the past few quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3: Different indicators of consumer price inflation; Chart 3.4: CCPI rent component and market rents; Chart 3.5: Unit labour cost and wages per employee. Looking ahead, domestic inflation pressure should remain moderate in 2019, mainly reflecting weaker domestic growth momentum. However, earlier increases in private residential rents will continue to feed through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation for the full year is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. The above inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate has remained at around 2.8%, the lowest level in over 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap could turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if US–China trade frictions ease and the local economy performs better than expected, domestic inflation could be pushed up. Chart 3.6: Unemployment rate. The US–China trade conflict intensified gradually in the second half of 2018: the United States imposed 25% tariffs on US$34 billion and US$16 billion of imports from Mainland China on July 6 and August 23, respectively. In response to these two moves, Mainland China imposed 25% tariffs on an equivalent value of US goods. The United States further escalated the situation on September 24 by imposing a 10% tariff on US$200 billion of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US$60 billion of US goods. Since then, the two countries have engaged in negotiations to avoid further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has long served as a transshipment hub between these two economies, the imposition of tariffs is bound to have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the US–China trade dispute has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This special topic reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its short-term prospects. We will also attempt to use more granular data to identify trade goods directly affected by the imposition of tariffs, thereby examining the impact of the tariffs in greater detail. To analyse the impact of tariffs, we first extracted six groups of Hong Kong re-export data that were affected by the various rounds of tariff increases described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariff increases, the United States mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the range of affected goods expanded to include more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff increases as List 1, List 2, and List 3, respectively. After collecting this more granular trade data, we focused on analysing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong's re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. In addition, readers should exercise caution when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity in that month was disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the results of the analysis in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariff increases. Re-exports from Mainland China affected by tariffs: Shortly after the imposition of tariffs, the value of relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the United States appeared to have declined significantly or grown at a slower pace (Chart B3.1). For example, re-export growth for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the tariffs were imposed, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1: Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the United States in 2018. Re-exports from the United States affected by tariffs: In contrast, goods re-exported from the United States through Hong Kong to Mainland China showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports for List 1 appeared to have declined significantly in the months following the imposition of tariffs, but then rebounded towards the end of the year. Re-exports for List 2 remained in negative growth territory for most of the year, while growth for List 3 appeared to be broadly stable. Chart B3.2: Value of goods re-exported from the United States through Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018. Front-loading: Because there is sometimes a lag between the announcement and the actual implementation of tariffs (or simply because of the threat of tariff increases), businesses may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected date of tariff implementation. In fact, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour was quite common. Some private-sector analysts also believe that this behaviour was part of the reason for the strong overall trade figures before the tariff increases. More granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for certain tariff-list goods, but this appears to have involved only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the United States (Chart B3.1). The growth rates of re-exports for List 1 and List 2 increased in the months before the respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, the growth rates of goods re-exported from the United States through Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) showed no evidence of significant front-loading behaviour by businesses. Re-exports not affected by tariff increases: It is worth noting that re-exports (in value terms) directly affected by tariff increases accounted for only about 4% to 5% of total Hong Kong re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by tariff increases. We found that re-exports not affected by tariff increases recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). In addition, growth in re-exports affected by tariffs (red line) showed a significantly larger decline from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of tariffs. The slowdown in re-exports not affected by tariff increases partly reflects weaker external demand more broadly. As trade frictions continue to increase uncertainty, global financial conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks rise, external demand is likely to come under more widespread pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has dampened global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in corrections in major stock markets. Import demand in other economies has thus been affected, weighing on Hong Kong's external trade performance. Chart B3.3: Value of Hong Kong's re-exports in 2018. Even if US–China trade frictions ease, the short-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth is likely to slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further weigh on Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that businesses of all sizes are pessimistic about their business prospects (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trade sector being particularly weak. Other trade-related industries, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4: Business prospects survey for Hong Kong's import and export industries.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting expectations of seasonal funding demand that tightened liquidity and prompted the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the HKD exchange rate gradually weakened, owing in part to corporates repatriating proceeds from new equity offerings and to market participants rebuilding carry-trade positions, which triggered the weak-side convertibility undertaking in March. Nonetheless, HKD trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before easing in January 2019. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the ongoing US–China trade frictions, Brexit negotiations, and a more unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, HKD fund flows may become more volatile. If the HKD–USD interest rate differential remains wide, carry-trade activities could persist, causing the HKD to stay relatively weak for some time and potentially triggering the weak-side convertibility undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the linked exchange rate system. Following the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking in late August, the HKD exchange rate deviated from the 7.8500 level, fluctuating between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until March 2019, when the weak-side convertibility undertaking was triggered again for a total of four times (as of March 19) (Chart 4.1). The HKD exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, but subsequently fell gradually in October. The HKD stabilised again after November, as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity and led to the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates repatriating proceeds from new equity offerings and market participants rebuilding carry-trade positions. As the HKD–USD interest rate differential widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying USD and selling HKD, causing the HKD to weaken gradually and triggering the weak-side convertibility undertaking again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly.
