The Aggregate Balance has remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), and fell slightly to HK$70.9 billion after the weak-side convertibility undertaking was triggered in March (as of March 19). Outflows of HKD since April 2018 represent only a small fraction of the approximately HK$1 trillion that has flowed in since 2008. Chart 4.1: HKD Exchange Rate; Chart 4.2: HKD Fund Flow Indicator. The HKD nominal effective exchange rate index largely tracked movements in the USD and continued to rise over the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the very small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the HKD real effective exchange rate index, the latter moved broadly in line with the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. The latest balance of payments statistics show that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and heightened stock market volatility, outflows of equity securities investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting inflows of portfolio investment by non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both local and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the ongoing US–China trade frictions, Brexit negotiations, and a more unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, fund flow volatility may intensify. Moreover, the significant negative interest rate differential between the HKD and the USD could stimulate arbitrage activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the linked exchange rate system, the HKD exchange rate may weaken and could trigger the weak-side convertibility undertaking again. Both capital outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking are normal operations under the linked exchange rate system. Despite the continued US interest rate normalisation process and the repeated triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking between April and August, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD monetary base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the monetary base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while certificates of indebtedness, government-issued banknotes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The HKD monetary base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance fell slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). Chart 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. As for broader HKD money supply indicators, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased macroeconomic and financial uncertainties. Hong Kong’s broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year, but increased only marginally by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). HKD deposits, a major component of HKD M3, showed little change compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Within HKD deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to grow strongly, reflecting higher deposit rates. Corresponding asset analysis shows that the slowdown in HKD M3 growth was driven by changes in bank capital and reserves (included in "net other items"). Chart 4.5: HKD M3 and Changes in Its Corresponding Assets. Foreign-currency deposits grew at a faster pace in the second half of the year. USD deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign-currency deposit growth, as banks attracted more deposits after raising their preferential USD deposit rates (Chart 4.6). Other foreign-currency deposits grew slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with RMB deposits continuing to increase. Overall, total deposits of authorised institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% growth in the first half. Chart 4.6: Deposit Growth. Although the HKD monetary base and deposit size remained substantial, HKD interbank offered rates (HIBOR) began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term HIBOR, causing it to be more volatile than long-term HIBOR (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month HIBOR averaged 2.32% and 2.74% in December, respectively, about 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Entering 2019, HKD HIBOR generally fell as seasonal demand subsided. The 3-month and 12-month HIBOR averages fell to 1.65% and 2.39%, respectively, in February. Chart 4.7: HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates. The HKD yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the USD yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, the yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points, respectively, to 1.56% and 1.83% by the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8: Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average New Mortgage Lending Rate. Over the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average HKD funding cost for retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before falling back to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). Given the rise in funding costs, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the increase in the US federal funds rate target range in September. However, after the US federal funds rate target range was raised again in December, retail banks did not adjust their best lending rates further. On the other hand, the average new mortgage lending rate followed the best lending rate upward, standing at around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, USD interest rate trends, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as new equity subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of HKD interest rates. Given that the HKD monetary base remains substantial and the banking system holds a large amount of Exchange Fund Bills, the pace of HKD interest rate increases should be moderate, as banks can borrow HKD funds at the discount window using Exchange Fund Bills as collateral. Against the backdrop of escalating US–China trade frictions, both offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates have depreciated against the USD since early 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, amid optimism driven by the resumption of high-level US–China trade talks, offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore and offshore RMB was not significant over the review period. Chart 4.9: Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates. Currently, the ongoing US–China trade frictions have not yet had a major impact on funding conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore RMB HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month offshore RMB HIBOR hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, which may reflect recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how developments in US–China trade negotiations will affect liquidity in the offshore RMB interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10: Overnight and 3-Month Offshore RMB HIBOR. Pricing of Hong Kong’s offshore RMB funding pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. RMB customer deposits and certificate of deposit (CD) balances grew at a slightly faster pace than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising by 3.7% to RMB 657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by RMB customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and by 5.2% in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than individual customer deposits. However, CD balances fell further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced CD issuance and a relatively large number of CDs maturing in October.

Retail banking profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017, primarily driven by an increase in net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions also remained robust. Reflecting upward pressure on Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, the overall Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banks rose significantly, though it remained at a low level. Against a backdrop of uncertain external conditions, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November, and asset quality remains sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to continued uncertainty in US-China trade relations, a global economic slowdown, uncertainty regarding the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the impact of any further deterioration in external conditions on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets (ROA) increased from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the rise in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For the full year of 2018, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while ROA increased from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1: Retail banking profitability. The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2: Retail banking NIM. This largely reflected the further US interest rate hikes and the decline in Hong Kong dollar interbank liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side convertibility undertaking in August 2018, which continued to exert upward pressure on Hong Kong interbank funding costs in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period, as banks generally raised fixed deposit rates to secure stable, long-term funding. Furthermore, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks increased their prime rates and, accordingly, raised their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banks) increased from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December 2018, but remained at a low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3: Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, banks' average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 36 basis points, following an increase of 40 basis points in the first half of the year (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4: Licensed banks' Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and tenors. The cumulative increase in HIBOR exceeded the rise in banks' overall funding costs, which could have a positive impact on retail banks' mortgage loans that are benchmarked to HIBOR—a product that the industry has actively promoted in recent years. However, future improvements in NIM may become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached their cap rates, which are linked to the prime rate. Given the uncertainty regarding the timing of future prime rate increases, the continued upward trend in banks' funding costs amid US interest rate normalization could put pressure on overall NIM. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment could cloud banks' profitability outlook. In particular, continued uncertainty in US-China trade relations, against a backdrop of slowing global economic growth, could dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this situation leads to a significant decline in lending and a deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks' profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong, well above international minimum standards. As of the end of 2018, the aggregate capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further increased to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5: Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions. 1. Aggregate position. 2. From 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards cannot be directly compared with data up to December 2012. In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratio, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6: Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. As measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions increased from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions also increased from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. 1. Aggregate position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates that authorized institutions' funding positions are stable. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio for Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system's stable funding structure. As of the end of 2018, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions increased slightly from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9: Liability structure of all authorized institutions. 1. Due to rounding, figures may not add up to the total. 2. Figures represent percentages of total liabilities (including capital and reserves). 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined in the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at the end of the year (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio increased slightly from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at the end of the year, as Hong Kong dollar deposit growth lagged far behind that of Hong Kong dollar loans. Chart 5.10: Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. We estimate that, under a shock scenario of a parallel increase in interest rates of 200 basis points, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks' interest rate positions would amount to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty regarding the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11: Impact of interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks. 1. An interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard 200 basis point parallel interest rate shock on an institution's interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the effect on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the bank's total capital base. Against a backdrop of continued uncertainty in US-China trade tensions, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, following an increase of 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to slower growth in local loans (including loans and trade finance used in Hong Kong) and a decrease in loans used outside Hong Kong. Local loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half of the year, while loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth rates of 5.3% and 5.2%, respectively, in the previous six months. For 2018 as a whole, the growth rate of total loans slowed significantly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%. Chart 5.12: Loan growth. Looking ahead, credit demand is likely to remain weak in the short term. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Survey" conducted in December 2018 showed that 82% of all surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of authorized institutions expecting a decline in demand increased to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite a slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound. The total specific classification loan ratio and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions fell slightly to 0.55% and 0.36%, respectively, at the end of December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40%, respectively, at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the total specific classification loan ratio fell slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans rose slightly to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios are at low levels by historical standards. Chart 5.13: Asset quality of retail banks. 1. Specific classification loans refer to loans classified as "substandard," "doubtful," or "loss." 2. Figures prior to December 2015 reflect the situation of retail banks' Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks. On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to slower growth in personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal purpose loans), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a slower pace than personal loan growth, the ratio of household debt to GDP increased slightly from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has simultaneously impacted both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to mitigate the economic shock caused by the pandemic, financial markets remain volatile, and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets have continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. During the review period, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed, given the stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, stable aggregate balance, and moderate growth in total deposits. After a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, total loan growth slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though with some fluctuations. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should carefully assess the impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should they intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown tentative signs of stabilisation, supported by increased monetary easing by major central banks, a easing of US-China trade tensions, and a reduction in the risk of a "no-deal" Brexit. However, since late January, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide has heightened market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks posed by the pandemic, several major central banks have cut interest rates sharply and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions have tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp declines in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will weigh on global economic activity, with the extent of the impact depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners may once again become strained, and trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union following Brexit could prove challenging. Weak global demand continues to weigh on economic growth in East Asia. Exports from the region to major destinations, including the United States, European economies, and mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported earnings growth, but it remains to be seen whether the technology product cycle will experience a broad-based rebound. Financial markets reacted positively to the US-China Phase One trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce has reduced global trade uncertainties to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds from weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region’s economies may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region could adversely affect Asia’s tourism industry, particularly in economies that are more reliant on tourism service exports. Given the region’s close integration with mainland China’s supply chains, manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak. In mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the US-China Phase One trade agreement will help temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the mainland economy, downside pressures remain amid the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing, and a global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 identified economic stabilisation as a priority for 2020, while also emphasising the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that mainland China’s economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed to a possible decline in shareholders’ equity among private industrial enterprises in recent years, which is seen as a sign of "retrogression" in the private sector. Special Feature 2 examines the drivers of changes in equity among mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed company data and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more prone to contraction or "retrogression." While negative profitability was found to be the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural ones, are also noteworthy (see Special Feature 2 for details). Economic activity in Hong Kong contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP has declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy has entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, a sharp contrast to the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weakening domestic demand, particularly a decline in private consumption, was the main factor weighing on GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook and thereby reducing consumer and business confidence. Amid renewed escalation of US-China trade frictions, a slowdown in global economic growth, and a sharp decline in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained weak. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government introduced several rounds of stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To provide banks with greater scope to support the local economy more vigorously and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200–300 billion in lending capacity to businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the pandemic has recently introduced substantial downside risks. Since sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social events, the pandemic will deal a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessional low-interest loans for businesses under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" with 100% government guarantee. On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further lowered the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will provide banks with greater scope to support the local economy more vigorously, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the pandemic. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects reach completion. Regarding external factors, the US-China Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong’s export performance. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range from -1.5% to 0.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, US-China trade relations, mainland China’s economic performance, and local social events. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and the beginning of 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social events and the coronavirus outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Special Feature 3 will explore recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labour market in greater detail. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. Given weak economic conditions, stabilising private residential rents, and moderate import inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the short term. Market consensus forecasts that overall inflation in 2020 will range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate to be 2.5%. Supported by increased Hong Kong dollar demand related to equity activities (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. In December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate further intensified, partly due to robust IPO activity and partly due to short covering in Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened toward year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly toward the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly during the review period, and the Linked Exchange Rate system was not triggered. The aggregate balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as initial public offerings. Special Feature 4 examines how market expectations of future IPO activity affect the 3-month Hong Kong interbank offered rate (HIBOR). Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposits. As some banks raised the upper limits of rates set by the best lending rate (BLR), the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but as the BLR in the market was lowered from November onwards, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020. Given the stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, stable aggregate balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of a further deterioration in the coronavirus pandemic amid uncertainties in the external environment. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. During the review period, market expectations of a US-China trade agreement led to a strengthening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates, but they have faced downward pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the latter part of 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi; the discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool recovered slightly after a modest decline in the previous review period. As of the end of January 2020, renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances had increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Other renminbi businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with renminbi bank loans and renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong recording strong growth. The daily average transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-time Gross Settlement (RMB RTGS) system remained high at RMB 1.1339 trillion for the full year of 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of mainland China’s capital account, increased allocation of renminbi assets by international investors, and deepened regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives.

At the end of 2019, signs of stabilization in global economic activity raised market expectations of a worldwide recovery. However, since late January 2020, the surge in global coronavirus infections has dashed hopes of a rebound, deepening investors' concerns about a global recession and triggering sell-offs across global financial markets. To mitigate the economic shock, major central banks and several governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the global growth outlook have intensified. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has clouded the prospects for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional growth in the near term, with the tourism sector being particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asian economies continue to face challenges stemming from weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. In mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between the United States and China helps reduce external uncertainties temporarily, downside pressures persist amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a global slowdown; monetary and fiscal policy responses by authorities will provide some buffer. Amid continued trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth stayed sluggish in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilization in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier easing by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as a easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the US–China Phase One trade agreement. Chart 2.1: Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. However, since late January, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide and the subsequent economic shock have heightened market concerns, prompting a sell-off across global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that mainland China is a major export destination and plays a pivotal role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities there and the resulting drag on its economic growth will generate significant spillover effects, potentially affecting the entire globe (Chart 2.3). Since late February, a surge in coronavirus cases outside mainland China may exacerbate supply-chain disruptions and pose a direct risk to local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2: MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Aggregate Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread. Chart 2.3: Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China by Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (as a percentage of GDP). To address the potentially severe economic impact of the pandemic, some central banks (including the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) cut policy rates since early March, while several governments introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nevertheless, financial markets continued to face intense selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which could further exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4: Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for Advanced Economies. In addition to pandemic developments, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. Specifically, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have subsided following the US–China Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may prove challenging, as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are expected to be difficult, sustaining Brexit-related uncertainties. Moreover, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 due to sluggish global demand. Exports from East Asian economies to major destinations—including the United States, European economies, and mainland China—remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downturn in the region's technology products cycle may be bottoming out—including reports from major regional electronics firms of improved earnings at the end of 2019—it remains to be seen whether technology product exports will experience a substantive rebound.6 Chart 2.5: East Asia: Continued Weakness in Merchandise Exports to Major Destinations. Persistent weak growth and trade-related uncertainties have also dampened investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation falling in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which could affect the region's potential growth over the longer term. To support economic growth in a low-inflation environment, central banks in Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea cut policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after doing so in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6: East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. With many regional economies imposing entry restrictions on mainland China, the tourism sector has been hit hardest, particularly those economies more reliant on Chinese visitors and tourism service exports, which have suffered greater impacts from the pandemic (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensified pandemic will also affect regional supply chains closely linked to mainland China. Chart 2.7: East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Visitors. In the near term, the pandemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be short-lived, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government measures to contain it. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although markets expect corporate earnings to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), the globally accommodative monetary environment encourages yield-seeking behavior, driving asset prices higher without fundamental support. Consequently, regional equity markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8: Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents. Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it harder for private entities in the region to service their debt. While lower domestic interest rates can provide relief for indebted firms and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Additionally, as discussed in Special Topic 1, the influx of index-tracking funds into regional financial markets may exacerbate the risk of debt overhang for private entities, although this effect may be limited to financially stronger firms and their long-term borrowing. Third, regarding external factors, East Asian economies may face heightened risks amid increasingly protectionist US trade policies. Despite recent progress in the US–China Phase One trade agreement, trade tensions between the two countries persist, as fundamental trade issues remain unresolved. The widening trade surpluses of many regional economies with the United States (Chart 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations may continue to seek alternative sourcing routes outside China-centered supply chains to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging economies (excluding China) with the United States had risen to about US$167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to expand, the relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of trade disputes; for example, the US government imposed a massive 456% tariff on Vietnamese steel imports in July 2019.7 Given this, despite the US–China trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9: Merchandise Trade Surplus with the United States. Over the past decade, heightened integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-based funds.8 Index-based funds include not only those that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that use indices as benchmarks.9 By bringing in overseas investors that relevant economies might otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help foster the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, supporting long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, market concerns exist that investments by such funds may weaken the fiscal discipline of corporate bond issuers, leading to higher leverage levels for the firms involved.10 Furthermore, some argue that the growth of index-based funds in recent years has heightened volatility in global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common drivers—even more vulnerable.11 This Special Topic assesses the impact of index-based investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investments to relevant bonds according to the weights of constituent bonds within a benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds may reduce issuers of index constituents' incentives to act in the best interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks for the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1: Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies. Using the weights of firms from various emerging market economies within a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for the extent to which their bonds are held by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investments raises the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to fostering the development of emerging market corporate bond markets, the expanded long-term investor base resulting from passive bond fund investments also benefits emerging market firms. We also find that the above effect is significant only for emerging market firms with stronger fundamentals—particularly those with higher solvency and lower leverage ratios (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent firms appear less likely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investments. In summary, the above research indicates that growth in passive bond fund investments does not necessarily significantly increase solvency risks for the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Hong Kong’s economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009, owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending, and poor export performance. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the coronavirus outbreak has recently introduced substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is being shaped by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, US–China trade relations, economic performance in mainland China, and developments in local social events. Given the various headwinds confronting the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Domestic inflation pressure is expected to ease, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) shrank by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively (Table 3.A). As a result of the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, a sharp contrast to the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marked the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters, respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract markedly from the third quarter onward.33 Amid heightened economic uncertainty and a deterioration in business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and weighed on GDP in the fourth quarter.34 Externally, Hong Kong’s external trade performance continued to be sluggish, as US–China trade frictions intensified, global economic growth weakened, and visitor arrivals plummeted (Chart 3.2).35 Net exports subtracted from GDP in the third quarter due to a sharp contraction in service exports, but contributed to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance. Chart 3.2: Real imports and exports Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and hard-hit sectors such as retail, food services, transportation, and tourism.36 To provide banks with greater capacity to support the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200–300 billion in lending capacity to businesses, including SMEs. Hong Kong’s economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the outbreak has recently introduced substantial downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social events, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including one-off cash payments to adult permanent residents and concessional low-interest loans for businesses under the “SME Financing Guarantee Scheme” with 100% government guarantee.37 The HKMA further lowered the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will give banks greater capacity to support the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the outbreak. Analyzing GDP by component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects reach completion. Regarding external factors, the Phase One US–China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range from -1.5% to 0.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks outlined in previous chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and the beginning of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further increased to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Notably, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social events.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline, reaching 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was primarily concentrated in the import/export, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face further challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Special Topic 3 will explore recent developments and short-term prospects in the labor market in greater detail. Chart 3.3: Labor market conditions Domestic inflation pressure continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase moderating slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum and is measured on a three-month moving annual rate basis, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures across several components of the CCPI. For tradable goods, fresh pork price increases kept basic food inflation significant, although price pressures for consumer items such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained moderate. For services, as growth in newly signed private residential rents slowed, the growth of the rent component in the CCPI also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labor cost pressure rose slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4: Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5: CCPI rent component and market rents Chart 3.6: Unit labor cost Domestic inflation pressure is expected to ease in the short term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to moderate, the housing rent component of inflation should ease further. Externally, import inflation is expected to remain moderate due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts that overall inflation in 2020 will range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5% and overall inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in the economy (for example, due to a prolonged coronavirus outbreak) could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, a more severe disruption to fresh pork supplies would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the local economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as social events persisted that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this special topic analyzes recent developments and short-term prospects in the labor market, including why the overall labor market remained broadly resilient in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing), and what implications this holds for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labor demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate typically lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lag can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1: Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate Regarding labor demand, although US–China trade tensions and local social events dealt heavy blows to employment in trade- and retail- and tourism-related sectors, some major industries were able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social, and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting declines in employment in trade and retail (Chart B3.2). Despite the recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, and financial activities such as fintech development and new stock issuance were very active. These factors may have helped support employment in the financial and business services sectors. Furthermore, public administration, social, and personal services—including education, healthcare, and social work activities—appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of public administration, social, and personal services to the economic cycle is more neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Chart B3.2: Changes in employment by sector in 2019 Regarding labor supply, the labor force participation rate40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against rising unemployment. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, an increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted significantly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment fell during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped mitigate upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3: Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some changes in the structure of the labor market are also worth noting. In particular, an increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the share of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment has fallen to 6% and 1%, respectively, in recent years, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (around 7% in 2017).42 As a result, companies may be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the larger share of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum further intensifying in December, causing the currency to remain in the strong side of the convertibility undertaking range over recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar stems partly from stock-related demand and partly from the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar as liquidity tightens toward year-end. Overall, the operation of Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets has continued to be smooth and orderly. Although market sentiment triggered by the coronavirus outbreak could lead to greater volatility in capital flows amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong’s substantial foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system equip it to withstand pressure from capital outflows without compromising the city’s financial stability. Supported by increased Hong Kong dollar demand related to equities, including initial public offerings (IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar further intensified, and from mid-December through February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the convertibility undertaking range. The appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar was partly due to robust IPO activity and partly to the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar as liquidity tightened toward year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly during the review period. Since neither the strong-side nor the weak-side convertibility undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1: Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate; Chart 4.2: Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. The Hong Kong dollar’s nominal effective exchange rate index largely tracked movements in the US dollar, rising slightly during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the very small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the impact on the Hong Kong dollar’s real effective exchange rate index was limited, and its movement largely mirrored that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. When measuring capital flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts of capital flow: (1) Hong Kong dollar capital flow, and (2) cross-border capital flow. Hong Kong dollar capital flow focuses on the currency dimension of capital movements and helps assess monetary stability, particularly under the linked exchange rate system. Cross-border capital flow, on the other hand, focuses on the movement of funds across regions through Hong Kong’s banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong’s overall financial system. These two concepts of capital flow require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar capital flow, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large portion of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the linked exchange rate system, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side convertibility undertaking rate of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars from banks upon request, thereby reducing the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained largely unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed on the strong side of the convertibility undertaking range in recent months; therefore, no significant outflow of Hong Kong dollar capital was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. When there is a large outflow of funds from Hong Kong’s banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there was no significant cross-border capital outflow. The operation of Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets has continued to be smooth and orderly, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Hong Kong’s monetary environment remains limited. Nevertheless, we need to closely monitor the risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak. With substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained sizable, rising 4.0% since the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). Since the convertibility undertaking was not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund bills and notes, certificates of indebtedness, and circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, increased steadily. Chart 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, broad indicators of Hong Kong dollar money supply remained largely stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and then rose slightly by 0.2% over the seven months since the end of June 2019. A corresponding assets analysis shows that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June primarily reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and an expansion of the monetary base (driven by increases in certificates of indebtedness and circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven months since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained largely unchanged (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5: Hong Kong Dollar M3 and Changes in Corresponding Assets. Over the seven months since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits denominated in Hong Kong dollars recording a slight decline. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s overall broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5%, respectively, since the end of June (Chart 4.7). Since monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), the figures should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6: Deposits of Authorized Institutions by Currency; Chart 4.7: Broad Money Supply (M2). Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly heightened IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market. Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) for overnight funds experienced larger fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong interbank rates generally rose. Large new share listings and their subscription activities can exert significant pressure on overnight rates, and empirical analysis in Special Topic 4 shows that market attention to future IPO activity can also affect the 3-month Hong Kong interbank rate. This occurs when market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines for large new share listings and pre-position medium-term funds in advance. Chart 4.8: Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates. As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it followed the US dollar yield curve downward. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% as of February 28, 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9: Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Lending Rate for New Mortgages. At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks’ continued upward adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposits, thereby raising the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the reduction in the US federal funds rate target range at the end of October 2019, several retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, retail banks’ best lending rates currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. For mortgage loans, major banks raised the upper limit of rates set by reference to the best lending rate for mortgage loans benchmarked to Hong Kong interbank rates, causing the average lending rate for new mortgages in October to rise to around 2.63%.45 Since November, best lending rates in the market have been lowered, and the average mortgage lending rate has subsequently declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the federal funds rate target range by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on March 3 (US time) and March 15 (US time). Although Hong Kong interbank rates follow US interest rate movements over the longer term, short-term Hong Kong interbank rates may be influenced by local factors that could affect Hong Kong dollar demand, such as new share listing activity in Hong Kong. The Aggregate Balance in the banking system has declined since April 2018, which may have increased the sensitivity of Hong Kong interbank rates to changes in Hong Kong dollar funding supply and demand. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet banks’ payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. Should liquidity tighten in the short term, banks can utilize the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Given the potential escalation of the US-China trade conflict, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi against the US dollar falling to a decade-low of 7.19 on September 2 (Chart 4.10). Entering October, as markets anticipated a resumption of US-China trade negotiations, the renminbi’s depreciation trend reversed; offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and, following the signing of the US-China Phase One trade agreement, briefly rose above the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since late January, due to the coronavirus outbreak, offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced downward pressure. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, at a premium for much of late 2019, and the discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020; however, the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10: Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates. Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained largely stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank rate continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank rate experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to MSCI A-share adjustments and again at the end of January 2020 near the Lunar New Year holiday.

Amid heightened uncertainty in both the global and local economic environment, profitability at Hong Kong retail banks declined slightly in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remain strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remains healthy by historical benchmarks. Although overall loan growth slowed in the second half of the year, it still outpaced deposit growth over the same period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios (LDRs) for all authorized institutions, measured in all currencies and in Hong Kong dollars, both increased. However, given that the banking system’s aggregate balance has remained stable and deposits have largely held steady, the sector’s liquidity position stayed robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking industry will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, the future trajectory of US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should they intensify. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018.59 Accordingly, return on assets (ROA) edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), net interest income (NII) of retail banks continued to record modest growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses at retail banks led to a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1: Retail bank profitability; Chart 5.2: Retail bank net interest margin. Despite three 25-basis-point cuts to the US Federal Funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) wholesale funding market has not experienced significant downward pressure to date. On the contrary, short-term HKD interbank offered rates (HIBOR) have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, driven by several local factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large initial public offerings (IPOs), and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions. Meanwhile, longer-term HKD HIBOR rates remained largely stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months prior (the blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, given that HKD savings deposit rates remain near zero, retail banks have limited scope to follow the US policy rate cuts with further reductions.60 On the other hand, as HKD liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete to attract stable, long-term deposits.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of HKD deposits, the composite interest rate—an indicator of retail banks’ average HKD funding cost—gradually rose from 0.95% six months prior to 1.09% at the end of 2019, though it remains low by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3: Interest rates. From a broader perspective, given that the decline in licensed banks’ US dollar funding costs offset the slight increase in their HKD funding costs, the average overall HKD and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell marginally by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of HKD HIBOR rates, thereby supporting banking sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4: Licensed banks’ HKD and US dollar funding costs and tenors. 1. Starting from June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB) framework will submit returns under the new framework, while those exempted will continue to submit returns under the existing IRRBB framework. Overall funding costs and tenors have been calculated as weighted averages based on the figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onward cannot be directly compared with those from previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cast a shadow over banks’ profitability outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, the future trajectory of US-China trade relations, and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could weaken already fragile global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist, which could exert pressure on banks’ future net interest margins. Locally, social events since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against an already weak economic backdrop, a continuation or further escalation of the situation could worsen the outlook for credit demand and deteriorate bank asset quality. In terms of overall market developments, following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s (HKMA) issuance of eight virtual banking licences, the Hong Kong banking industry has begun to roll out virtual banking services. As these new market entrants may seek to increase their market share by attracting new customers through more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this could put upward pressure on existing banks’ funding costs. While the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks’ operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of fintech to remain competitive. The findings of Special Topic 5 indicate that the extent of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in cost efficiency and enhancements in profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains robust and well above the minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the aggregate capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further increased to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5: Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, the Basel III non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement serves to limit excessive leverage in the banking system.
