The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6: Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. Measured by the Basel III “Liquidity Coverage Ratio” (LCR) requirement,65 the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) for Category 2 institutions also increased modestly from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also far exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR),66 as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates the stability of authorized institutions’ funding profiles. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions remained high at 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio for Category 2A institutions remained high at 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and stable funding profile of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system’s stable funding structure. At the end of 2019, customer deposits as a proportion of total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained largely unchanged, falling slightly from 56.4% six months prior to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9: Liability structure of all authorized institutions. The average HKD LDR of all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), as HKD loans and advances remained largely stable while deposits declined slightly during the review period.67 Meanwhile, the average foreign currency LDR also increased from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period, driven by faster growth in foreign currency loans relative to deposits. Overall, the average LDR of all authorized institutions, measured in all currencies, rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of that year. Given that the banking system’s aggregate balance has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have largely held steady, there were no apparent signs of significant outflows of funds from the HKD market or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Chart 5.10: Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. Interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that, under a shock scenario of a 200-basis-point increase in HKD and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would amount to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11: Impact of HKD and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against a backdrop of US-China trade tensions, a global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social events, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a modest rebound in the first half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by changes in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) increased modestly by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to a deceleration in both local loans (including loans and trade finance used in Hong Kong) and loans used outside Hong Kong during the review period. Local loans and loans used outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively, in the second half of 2019, lower than the 4.5% and 3.5% growth recorded in the first half. Nevertheless, overall loan growth for 2019 still rose modestly to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% recorded for the full year of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has raised hopes for an economic restart and improved the outlook for global growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainty, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the lasting economic scars caused by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets have continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar has traded close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level against the US dollar, driven mainly by stock-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of large-scale outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand due to recurring waves of the pandemic, total bank loans declined slightly in the second half of the year, although they still recorded a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market has remained largely stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of businesses and households, and the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of related downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but growth slowed again from the fourth quarter as COVID-19 infection numbers rose. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expect the pandemic to eventually end, which should help the global economy return to normal and accelerate growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect with the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be distributed widely. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which may in turn force central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier than anticipated, ending market expectations of a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy stance. In the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address a range of economic legacies left by the pandemic, including high global debt levels and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a rebound in export demand. Against a backdrop of increased risk appetite, inflows of portfolio investment into the region rebounded, and yield-seeking activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces continued uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity amid global competition for vaccine procurement, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service industries. Second, variability in vaccine supply, coverage, or effectiveness, coupled with weakening fiscal positions in the region, could sour market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. In mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will still depend largely on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecasts show that the mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months at the beginning of 2020, but then strengthened for the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and the mainland bond market recorded strong capital inflows. Detailed research shows that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations (see Special Feature 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. As domestic demand picked up slightly and merchandise exports expanded further, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that the economy has contracted for two consecutive years, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related sectors was worse than that of the overall economy during the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-Epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help industries and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's capacity to combat the epidemic. The government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal loans for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the "Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism," also announced in March 2021 that the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme would be extended to October of that year and that the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme would be extended. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines are expected to enable a return to normal economic activity, and the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole). However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be affected by many uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2021 will be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private sector analysts average 4.4%. The labor market situation deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and the beginning of 2021. The unemployment rate rose further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To address the worsening labor market situation, the government launched the "Job Retention Scheme" under the second round of the Anti-Epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain employees. After the "Job Retention Scheme" ended, the government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund to further support industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Special Feature 2 discusses the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labor market. Local inflationary pressure continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021, respectively. The underlying inflation rate, measured on a three-month moving average annualized basis, which reflects inflation momentum, has fluctuated slightly in recent months but has remained at a low level. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressure in Hong Kong is likely to remain mild in the short term, particularly as local inflation will continue to be restrained by slower growth in newly signed private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate in 2021 will be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the government forecasts that the underlying and overall inflation rates in 2021 will be 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The Hong Kong dollar has traded close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level against the US dollar, driven mainly by stock-related funding demand, including demand from robust new share issuance activities and southbound inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect). Funding activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain strong. During the review period, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with HK$263.3 billion flowing into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with a cumulative inflow of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. From a regional perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating that there were no signs of large-scale outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the evolution of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued US-China tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding capital flow volatility. As the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered, increasing the aggregate balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. As funding costs fell, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 basis points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances increasing to RMB 826.3 billion as of the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi businesses, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while renminbi trade settlement increased, with the average daily transaction volume of the renminbi real-time gross settlement system remaining high at RMB 1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous channels for cross-border capital flows to the mainland. As the mainland's capital account continues to open up, international investors' demand for renminbi assets increases, and regional economic and financial cooperation deepens under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by rising global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors through the Stock Connect scheme, the Hong Kong stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global stock markets rose due to unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism about positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period, and briefly surpassed the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing large net outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence quickly recovered as governments around the world introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures, and inflows of bond funds into the local market rebounded. Although bond yields rebounded moderately over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historic lows.

As breakthroughs were made in vaccine development, markets expected the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually end, allowing the global economy to grow at an accelerated pace thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a "longer period of low interest rates" in global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the pandemic resurgence at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the lofty expectations of financial markets are at odds with a still challenging macroeconomic environment; should the economic recovery fall short of expectations or policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the dilemma of when to withdraw policy support and will need to address numerous issues left in the pandemic's wake, including high debt levels and lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, where emerging market economies with slower development may face greater challenges in procuring and distributing vaccines. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programs could reverse the current optimism and destabilize capital inflows and financial markets. In mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking forward, the outlook for economic growth remains highly uncertain, largely depending on the evolution of the pandemic and developments in U.S.–China tensions. Accordingly, the government announced that it would maintain its supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by the economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection numbers have risen again, prompting governments worldwide to reinstate lockdown and social distancing measures, causing global growth momentum to weaken once more. At the end of 2020, more contagious variants emerged and subsequently spread across the globe, further exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use by the end of 2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normal and grow at an accelerated pace. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery stems from continued policy stimulus measures, including major central banks' commitment to a "longer period of low interest rates" amid weak inflation, as well as ongoing fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the U.S. Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 projection (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1: Real GDP growth forecasts by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, with cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery seeing rising stock prices, driving global equities and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2: 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios for major stock indices. However, while financial markets have performed strongly, the macroeconomic environment remains challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control hinges on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, overall global vaccination rates were still low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX aim to promote more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supply is likely to exacerbate low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies. If the pandemic is not brought under control as expected, regions may need to maintain social distancing and other restrictions, thereby undermining the outlook for global recovery. Chart 2.3: Share of population that has received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of March 15, 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets has been predicated on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly a "longer period of low interest rates." However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn at a faster pace than anticipated. For example, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have already risen due to a combination of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing (Chart 2.4). If inflation proves stronger than expected in the future, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4: 5-year/5-year forward inflation-linked swap rates for the United States and the eurozone. Third, there is significant uncertainty regarding the future of U.S.–China relations. The trend of "decoupling" between the United States and China, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States toward mainland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in U.S.–China tensions could trigger turmoil in financial markets in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing these measures too early could jeopardize the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," the costs of maintaining them over the long term are high, including fiscal burdens and delays in the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic, such as allowing "zombie firms" whose business models are no longer viable to continue operating with government support. Additionally, policymakers must address numerous issues left in the pandemic's wake. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending (Chart 2.5). Although the problems posed by the rapid rise in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5: Global debt as a share of GDP. Another lingering issue concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, heightened uncertainty may lead firms to reduce investment, while workers who remain unemployed for extended periods may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth rebounded in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The driving force behind the economic recovery was primarily a rebound in exports, with demand for electronics and technology equipment being particularly strong. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face interaction with customers, continued to struggle. Chart 2.6: East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020. Despite lingering uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have flowed back into the region. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production plans were launched, equity inflows to East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Currencies in the region have also appreciated in response to portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by about 10% from its lowest point in March of last year. Chart 2.7: East Asia: Portfolio investment flows. The East Asian region continues to face persistent uncertainty related to the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offers hope for the region's hard-hit service sectors and economies, competition worldwide for early batches of vaccines has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. Consequently, economies in the region with slower development may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, given that investors' optimism has been largely driven by the rollout of vaccines, if vaccination progress or effectiveness falls far short of expectations, the current inflows of capital and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. As COVID-19 was successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovered, the mainland Chinese economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports also continued to grow, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-tech goods (Chart 2.8). Overall, in 2020, despite facing an unprecedented shock from the COVID-19 pandemic, mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8: Mainland China: Contributions to GDP growth by demand component. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the mainland Chinese economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be a major driver of economic growth. However, whether the economy can sustain its recovery will still depend, to some extent, on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the mainland have returned to normal, the service sector continues to face some disruptions as outbreaks have reemerged in several northern provinces. Externally, while exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to renewed outbreaks in most developed economies. Additionally, U.S.–China tensions may not ease in the short term, but the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the agreed-upon Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the European Union could help China further integrate with other economies, potentially offsetting some of the adverse effects of U.S.–China decoupling on the economic recovery. Given that the economic outlook remains highly uncertain, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that its existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Furthermore, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identifies technological self-reliance and the "dual circulation" strategy as priority development directions, with the aim of achieving a per capita GDP level comparable to that of a moderately developed country by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment capacity of bond-issuing enterprises appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in the mainland Chinese bond market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 due to a sharp rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) (Chart 2.9). While the increase in SOE defaults primarily reflects the central government's determination to break the "rigid repayment" guarantee for SOEs in order to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, limited fiscal space for some local governments, particularly those in less developed regions, may also be a contributing factor. Chart 2.9: Mainland China: Size and proportion of onshore bond defaults. In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, especially for high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalization of interest rates contributed to some extent to higher financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events in the final quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10: Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields. In the real estate market, housing prices in mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, price increases in lower-tier cities were much slower (Chart 2.11). Meanwhile, the problem of oversupply in third-tier cities that plagued them in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months recorded in early 2015.

Although real GDP remains well below pre‑pandemic levels, the Hong Kong economy showed improvement in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand recovered and merchandise exports expanded further. With expectations that COVID‑19 vaccination will enable a return to normal economic activity, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume growth in 2021, following the most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be affected by numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the Hong Kong economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. Accordingly, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the short term, while domestic inflationary pressures should stay mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained far below pre‑pandemic levels. The year‑on‑year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest drop on record and the first time the economy has contracted for two consecutive years since a 1.2% decline in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry also show that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors recorded year‑on‑year declines in recent quarters, with the contraction being more pronounced in consumption‑ and tourism‑related industries than in the overall economy. On a quarter‑to‑quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending a five‑quarter consecutive decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, but consumer confidence remained weak as authorities re‑imposed social distancing measures amid the third and fourth waves of the pandemic domestically. Overall investment spending also increased in the second half of the year, reflecting a temporary improvement in business sentiment. Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further, partly benefiting from stronger export performance, especially to mainland China (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak, as the global tourism industry stayed stagnant. Overall, net imports (a trade deficit) subtracted from GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting that the rebound in merchandise exports lagged behind that of imports. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure components; Chart 3.2: Real imports and exports. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti‑Epidemic Fund, totalling HK$30.4 billion, between September and December 2020, to assist pandemic‑affected industries and individuals and to enhance Hong Kong’s capacity to combat the epidemic. The Government also announced additional counter‑cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one‑off electronic consumption voucher of HK$5,000 and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal loans for the unemployed. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 that the “Pre‑approved Principal Payment Holiday” scheme would be extended until October of that year, and that the repayment period for trade‑finance loans under the scheme would also be extended. These extensions are expected to help alleviate cash‑flow difficulties faced by some business customers. With COVID‑19 vaccines expected to enable a return to normal economic activity, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), although the strength and pace of the recovery will be affected by numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s merchandise and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large‑scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts that real GDP growth for 2021 as a whole will be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private analysts average 4.4%. Labour‑market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and in early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17‑year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, a post‑SARS high. Total employment fell to a low before stabilising (Chart 3.3), and government figures show that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average wage index for employees, which reflects labour income, slowed to 2.0% year‑on‑year in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address the worsening labour‑market situation, the Government introduced the “Employment Support Scheme” under the second round of the Anti‑Epidemic Fund, providing time‑limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. After the scheme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one‑off allowances) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti‑Epidemic Fund to provide further support to industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Special Topic 2 examines the potential impact of the boom and bust in inbound tourism on the local labour market. Chart 3.3: Labour‑market conditions; Chart 3.4: Different indicators of consumer price inflation. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid‑2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year‑on‑year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 (Chart 3.4). The underlying inflation rate, measured on a three‑month moving‑average annualised basis and reflecting inflation momentum, has also remained low despite some volatility in recent months. Specifically, price pressures for basic foodstuffs have eased, and the cost of dining out has fallen markedly, reflecting that more restaurants offered take‑out discounts during periods when dine‑in services were restricted. Price pressures for other traded goods, such as durables, have remained moderate. In the services sector, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index has remained weak as private residential rents have stabilised (Chart 3.5). Labour‑cost pressures have also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5: Rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and market rents; Chart 3.6: Unit labour cost. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, domestic inflationary pressures should stay mild in the short term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be restrained, partly due to slower growth in newly signed private residential leases. The market consensus forecasts overall inflation in 2021 to be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government projects underlying inflation of 1% and overall inflation of 1.6% for 2021. As the COVID‑19 pandemic took hold, inbound tourism quickly collapsed, raising concerns that the crisis could have scarring effects on the future recovery of the labour market. This Special Topic therefore provides an empirical analysis of the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on the Hong Kong labour market, in order to explore the potential implications of the current tourism downturn. Since 2000, inbound tourism to Hong Kong has experienced large fluctuations (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitors to Hong Kong declined during the 2003 SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak. Following the launch of the “Individual Visit Scheme” (IVS) in July of that year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original IVS, mainland residents could apply individually for one to two visits per year, each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible residents holding Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple‑entry “Individual Visit” visas (multiple‑entry permits). Since then, the number of mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross‑border infrastructure linking mainland China, visitor numbers reached a historic high in late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events caused visitor numbers to halve in the second half of 2019, and the COVID‑19 pandemic has left inbound tourism stagnant since late January 2020. Chart B2.1: Visitor numbers and related policies. We use the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as a case study to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We treat the IVS introduced in 2003 as a quasi‑random economic shock because its implementation was largely exogenous in timing and could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our primary data source is population data from the Hong Kong Population Census or By‑census. Specifically, we use the 5% sample from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By‑censuses. In addition, we define tourism‑related industries as catering, retail, hotels and transportation. First, we adopt a “difference‑in‑differences” (DiD) framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between a “treatment group” of younger workers (aged 20–40) and a “comparison group” of older workers (aged 41–65). We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because they are still at an early stage of their careers and can more flexibly adjust their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. Since the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market may vary over time, we also employ an “event‑study” approach to identify time‑varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism‑related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young women entering tourism‑related industries was both significant and persistent, remaining at around 5 percentage points (relative to the average difference in entry probability for the older cohort) since 2006 (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare earnings between those employed in tourism‑related industries (treatment group) and those in non‑tourism‑related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that, after the implementation of the IVS, workers in tourism‑related industries experienced higher earnings growth than employees in non‑tourism‑related industries. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and those with lower educational attainment in tourism‑related industries saw larger and increasing earnings gains (3–20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2: Impact of the IVS on female employment; Chart B2.3: Impact of the IVS on earnings of female and low‑education workers. The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, indicating that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, which showed that strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower‑skill labour and improved the robustness of the lower‑skill labour market. As inbound tourism moves from boom to bust, these groups of workers may be more adversely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level, which was triggered on multiple occasions between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was primarily driven by equity-related funding needs, including those arising from robust new share issuance activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance rose to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) fell across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in US-China relations may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand pressures arising from such volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including those from robust new share issuance activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some of the proceeds from initial public offerings (IPOs) were repatriated, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate fluctuated within a narrow band of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, owing to an improvement in market sentiment in the local stock market and expectations of rising funding demand toward year-end. As fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, which reflected substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the Aggregate Balance to rise from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 85 times in 2020 as a whole, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of large-scale outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any abnormal capital movements. Chart 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2: Equity funds raised on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK); Chart 4.3: Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index generally declined, tracking the weakness of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). Given the very small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate index, the latter moved largely in line with the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4: Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in US-China relations may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As an international financial center, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (such as new share issuance), resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently flow out of Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the monetary base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking. Meanwhile, other components—including Certificates of Indebtedness, circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes—remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5: Components of the monetary base. During the review period, large-scale new share issuance activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise significantly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As new share issuance activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased again substantially, mainly driven by large-scale new share issuance activities at the end of the month. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7% over the seven months since the end of June; excluding the impact of the new share issuance activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. Based on the corresponding assets analysis, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was primarily driven by the increase in the monetary base resulting from triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking (Chart 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of the new share issuance activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined due to low deposit rates, this was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6: Deposits of authorized institutions by currency; Chart 4.7: Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and corresponding assets. Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits fell slightly by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period, owing to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by new share issuance activities (Chart 4.6). Excluding the new share issuance activities at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal funding demand related to IPOs and business and investment-related activities); therefore, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. As the Aggregate Balance increased, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale new share issuance activities in the second half of 2020, HIBOR did not experience significant volatility, owing to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8: Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. The Hong Kong dollar yield curve largely followed the trend of the US dollar yield curve, becoming steeper during the review period as short-term bond yields fell while long-term bond yields rose (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9: Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average new mortgage lending rate. Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level mainly followed the decline in Hong Kong dollar HIBOR. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Owing to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, largely tracking the movement of the 1-month Hong Kong dollar HIBOR. Meanwhile, the best lending rates offered by retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the United States, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should remain low, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffer to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), largely reflecting better economic prospects in mainland China compared with other parts of the world, as well as US dollar weakness. FTSE Russell's announcement in late September that it would include mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index further supported renminbi strength through investment demand. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10: Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates. During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand toward year-end, it stayed below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR followed onshore renminbi rates in falling in late December, then rose again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11: Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR. In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool continued to expand. Since the fourth quarter, renminbi deposit growth has accelerated, partly reflecting renminbi appreciation and higher renminbi interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the growth rate of renminbi customer deposits and Certificates of Deposit (CDs) accelerated, reaching RMB 826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of this, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, CD balances fell by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12: Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong. As for other renminbi businesses, renminbi loan balances fell by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion over the seven months since the end of June 2020. On the other hand, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. Over the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, the transaction volume handled by local banks reached RMB 3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% year-on-year. Among the relevant transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the mainland grew at a faster pace than remittances from the mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong possesses a large renminbi funding pool, which is sufficient to continue supporting a high volume of renminbi payment and financial transactions. In 2020 as a whole, the daily average transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB 1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB 1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Owing to the continued economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with the impact of a prolonged low interest rate environment, Hong Kong’s retail banks saw a further decline in profitability and a slight deterioration in asset quality in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, the banking sector in Hong Kong remained resilient, supported by its strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) decided to extend several relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the challenging period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties, together with ongoing geopolitical tensions, will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking industry. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of businesses and households, and the banking industry should remain vigilant about the impact of related downside risks on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets (ROA) declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, down from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that outweighed the modest increase in non-interest income and led to a fall in profitability. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and ROA declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1: Profitability of retail banks; Chart 5.2: Net interest margin of retail banks. Largely driven by substantial capital inflows resulting from stock market activity, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) weakened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the 3-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The trend of the composite interest rate—an indicator of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banks—was broadly similar, falling significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and the reduction of time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3: Interest rates. From a broader perspective, the average overall funding cost in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars for licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4: Funding costs and maturities of licensed banks for Hong Kong dollars and US dollars. Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking industry will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks’ net interest margin performance. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain, given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking industry in the near term. The capital position of Hong Kong’s banking industry remains strong and is well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio was 16.7%, and the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, above the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5: Capital position of locally incorporated authorized institutions; Chart 5.6: Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. In terms of liquidity, the banking industry’s liquidity position remained strong during the review period, as measured by the “Liquidity Coverage Ratio” (LCR) requirement under Basel III. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Over the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The latest figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also indicate that authorized institutions’ funding position is stable. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio for Category 2A institutions remained high at 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%, respectively. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong’s banking industry is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9: Liability structure of all authorized institutions. As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased over the same period, the average loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all authorized institutions across all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency deposits. Accordingly, the average Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio and foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, at the end of 2020, down from 86.4% and 65.5%, respectively, six months earlier. Chart 5.10: Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200 basis point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would amount to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11: Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against the backdrop of a continued economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances fell modestly in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, the banking industry’s total credit still recorded positive growth, although the growth rate slowed significantly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions grew by 3.0% in the first half of 2020 but fell by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both local loans (including loans and trade finance used in Hong Kong) and loans used outside Hong Kong. In particular, total local loans fell slightly by 0.9% in the second half of the year, while total loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, in the previous six months. Chart 5.12: Loan growth. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after falling by 2.0% in the first half of the year, remained broadly at the same level at the end of 2020 as at the end of June. Foreign currency loans, after growing strongly by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, fell by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking industry’s outlook for short-term credit demand has turned slightly more optimistic compared with six months ago. The HKMA’s “Credit Conditions Survey” in December 2020 showed that the proportion of responding authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). The quality of banks’ loans deteriorated slightly due to the adverse impact of the pandemic on the repayment capacity of households and companies, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The total specific classification loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose modestly from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the total specific classification loan ratio and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy exhibited weak performance, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across various regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of a large-scale pandemic resurgence and the possibility that monetary policy tightening could exceed expectations if U.S. inflation proves more persistent and widespread than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve significantly tighten monetary policy, leading to a tightening of global financial conditions, this would exert pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has erupted, which could have a substantial impact on the global economy through trade and financial channels and further complicate the outlook for global monetary policy. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately over the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. For the full year of 2021, overall bank lending growth accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could threaten the sustainability of economic recovery, and the pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected; these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, with weakness persisting into 2022, owing to increased global mobility restrictions caused by the highly contagious Omicron variant and continued production pressures from supply bottlenecks. Meanwhile, global inflationary pressures have continued to intensify amid supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, spreading to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Recently, the surge in commodity prices following the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, complicating the outlook for global monetary policy. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainty. In the short term, a large-scale pandemic outbreak could not be ruled out, potentially leading to the reimposition of lockdown measures and a further deterioration of supply bottlenecks. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and widespread than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has adopted a hawkish stance, accelerating its timeline for reducing asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, and disorderly capital outflows could exert pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of continued increases, exacerbating shortages in industrial supplies and heightening financial market volatility. Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, raising their liquidity risk. Special Topic 1 will examine whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce these funds' liquidity risk during periods of market stress, and will discuss the tool's potential limitations. In Emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although the recovery momentum in some Southeast Asian economies slowed temporarily in the third quarter due to the reimposition of strict pandemic control measures, while technology-product exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although markets generally expect a broad-based recovery in Emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new virus variants remain a concern, especially for economies with lower vaccination rates and limited public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve's accelerated policy normalization could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures; economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. Third, a slowdown in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, the rise in various commodity prices triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will feed through to regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making process for monetary policy normalization by regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors will need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Special Topic 2 studies the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms' environmental performance. China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term due to the continued weakness in the property market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant. Consequently, the mainland authorities have made stabilizing growth their top priority for the year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Total onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both declined in the second half of 2021; Special Topic 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, low non-performing loan ratios, and high loan loss provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately, supported by goods exports and private consumption, which benefited from the continued recovery of the global economy, improvements in the local labor market, and the government's consumption voucher scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures have exerted pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Guaranteed Personal Loan Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the banking industry, will also extend the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year option to make partial principal repayments, which also applies to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme." Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery for the full year of 2022, but growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various infrastructure and public works projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2022 will be between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery will be influenced by various uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization. As the economy recovered, the labor market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end. Overall employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labor market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks. Additionally, a decline in the number of online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. A new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and tightened anti-pandemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labor market in the short term, particularly in industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate rose slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The underlying inflation rate, measured on a three-month annualized basis and reflecting inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly due to rising prices for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term as import prices increase and logistics are disrupted by the pandemic. However, weak rental growth and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate in 2022 will reach 2.4%, while the government expects the overall inflation rate in 2022 to be 2.1% and the underlying inflation rate to be 2.0%. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the U.S. dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar briefly rebounded in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak net southbound inflows via Stock Connect and weak market expectations that the U.S. dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalizes its monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained mostly within the strong side of the convertibility undertaking range, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately over the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Given ample interbank liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Offshore RMB banking business continued to thrive. In particular, Hong Kong's offshore RMB pool continued to grow, with RMB customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances increasing to RMB 1,113.5 billion as of the end of January 2022. Although RMB loan balances decreased, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily transaction volume of the RMB Real-time Gross Settlement System in 2021 rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the mainland's capital account, increased demand for RMB assets from international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, supported by Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Wealth Management Connect schemes.
