Fueled by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery, and strong corporate earnings, major global stock markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, driving the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. However, growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, sharp rises in commodity prices, and escalating Russia-Ukraine tensions have led to a consolidation in major global stock markets since early January 2022.

The global economy slowed markedly in the latter half of 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022, owing to the rapid spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron) worldwide and persistent production bottlenecks. Global inflationary pressures have continued to intensify and have broadened to encompass a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Heightened inflation concerns have prompted a hawkish shift in the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy stance, increasing the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations and hinder recovery in emerging markets, where progress remains uneven. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, exacerbating some of these risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with major technology-exporting economies in the region continuing to outperform others. Although the Omicron variant is unlikely to severely disrupt the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region’s economic outlook. In addition, the Fed’s policy normalization could trigger asset price adjustments in the region, while slower growth in major economies could weigh on the region’s merchandise export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine will both push up commodity prices and increase inflation risks, and weaken consumption and heighten global economic uncertainty, making monetary policy normalization decisions for regional central banks more complex. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from a cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the government has made stabilizing growth its top priority for the year, and macroeconomic policies will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed significantly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of Delta, triggering a new wave of infections and prompting tighter restrictions on movement worldwide. In addition, supply-chain problems—such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs like semiconductors—continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and slower growth in mainland China offsetting an expected rebound in other parts of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1: IMF Real GDP Growth Projections. Amid the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to build during the review period. Core inflation (which excludes food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the United States, which has implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic began. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices for a variety of commodities, which could exacerbate already high global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2: Core Consumer Price Index Inflation Rates in Selected Economies (1) The latest data for the United States, the United Kingdom, and the euro area are for January 2022; for others, they are for December 2021. (2) “Advanced economies in Asia” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) “Emerging market economies in Asia” include mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainty, with downside risks predominating, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply-chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy response of major central banks to inflation. With regard to the pandemic, most governments have so far taken targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these more relaxed measures should help reduce supply-chain disruptions, which have already shown preliminary signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should large-scale outbreaks occur, it cannot be ruled out that lockdown measures will be reimposed, which would then cause supply bottlenecks to worsen again. Chart 2.3: Purchasing Managers’ Index – Supplier Delivery Times Diffusion Index. If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to improve gradually, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current high level of global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices; the fact that rising production costs will feed through to final selling prices with a lag; the possibility that earlier sharp increases in global residential property prices could drive up rents going forward; upside risks to wage growth from tight labor markets; and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that U.S. inflation has recorded its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its Federal Open Market Committee meeting in December 2021, no longer characterizing high inflation as “transitory,” and doubling the pace of asset-purchase reductions from $15 billion to $30 billion per month, with the aim of ending the asset-purchase program by March 2022 and beginning discussions on balance-sheet reduction. In fact, recent market pricing indicates that the Fed may raise interest rates several times in 2022. By contrast, given the eurozone’s closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, and with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated after a prolonged period of accommodative policies, if inflationary pressures persist and cause the Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity could deteriorate, and financial market volatility could be triggered. Recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have escalated, risk aversion in financial markets has increased, and signs of dollar shortages have emerged, including widening cross-currency swap spreads. Under conditions of premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Special Topic 1 will examine whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce these funds’ liquidity risk when markets are under stress, and will discuss the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). At the same time, as major exporters of technology products in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, which further widened the unevenness of recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures remained moderate in several emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4: Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index. The market generally expects emerging markets in Asia to recover broadly in 2022, but the region’s short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: first, although the Omicron variant has spread in the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been milder than previous waves of infection; however, economies in the region with lagging vaccination rates and more limited public health resources will continue to face threats from the emergence of new variants. Second, the Fed’s policy normalization could trigger capital outflows and put depreciation pressure on regional currencies. For economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. In the long end of the yield curve, because the two have been highly correlated in the past (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in U.S. long-term yields will also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, increasing the risk of asset-market adjustments in the region. Chart 2.5: Correlation between Asian 10-Year Sovereign Bond Yields and Corresponding U.S. Treasury Yields. Third, the outlook for merchandise trade in the region faces uncertainty from slower growth in major economies and the possibility that demand will shift from goods to services as the global economy reopens, which could weaken export growth in the region. Chart 2.4: United States: Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP. Fourth, although economies in the region have limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will feed through to regional inflation and simultaneously weaken consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, this will make monetary policy normalization decisions for regional central banks more complex. Central banks in some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also serves as a reminder that economies in the region will need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in the long run to prepare for other risks, such as climate change. To this end, investors will need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Special Topic 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms’ environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced large outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1: Outflows from Selected Open-Ended Funds During the March 2020 Event. In addition to investors’ liquidity needs, another reason for large outflows may be that investors exercised “first-mover advantage” by redeeming funds early to avoid bearing redemption costs that could rise sharply in stressed market conditions. To curb outflows caused by first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds have adopted swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this event, there is no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing effectively reduces outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this special topic conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 event, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. In addition, this special topic will identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing when markets are under stress. Based on these assessments, we will make policy recommendations for financial stability. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming shares ahead of other investors, thereby shifting redemption costs onto them. First-mover advantage primarily exists in open-ended funds that use traditional pricing rules, whereby the costs of subscriptions and redemptions for fund investors (e.g., transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund’s price after the transaction takes place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are expected. Therefore, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced when markets are under stress, as redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by open-ended funds.

With continued growth in merchandise exports and private consumption, Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, achieving positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local COVID-19 infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures have exerted pressure on economic activity in the city. The overall economy is expected to maintain its recovery for the full year of 2022, although the pace and strength of this recovery will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and the normalization of U.S. monetary policy. These adverse factors could also impact the labor market outlook, which had improved significantly in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the short term due to higher import prices, weak local rents and labor costs should contain overall price pressures. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew by a further 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth slowed compared to the first half of the year. For the full year of 2021, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure components. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew modestly by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, an improvement in labor market conditions, coupled with the government's consumption voucher scheme, drove an increase in private consumption. However, overall investment spending declined in the final quarter after two consecutive quarters of strong rebound. Externally, Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance remained strong as the global economy continued to recover, while trade in services remained weak, partly because inbound tourism remained stagnant (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade weighed on GDP growth in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2: Import and export volumes. A new wave of local COVID-19 infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures have exerted pressure on economic activity in the city at the beginning of 2022. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Guaranteed Personal Loan Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the banking industry, has also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year option to repay part of the principal, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme." Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery for the full year of 2022, although the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global economic growth due to the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various public works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2022 will be between 2.0% and 3.5%, while growth forecasts from international organizations and private sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties and risks outlined in previous chapters. In particular, recent developments in the pandemic, the accelerated pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, if Hong Kong resumes quarantine-free travel with mainland China earlier than expected, it could stimulate local economic growth. As the economy recovered, the labor market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, although it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labor market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of local COVID-19 infections. Additionally, a decline in the number of online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, a new wave of local COVID-19 infections and tightened anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labor market in the short term, particularly in industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of local economic recovery. Chart 3.3: Labor market conditions. Local inflationary pressures have increased somewhat in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate rose slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The underlying inflation rate, measured on a three-month moving average annualized basis, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, prices for dining out and some energy-related items have risen faster as local demand recovers and external prices increase (Chart 3.5). Meanwhile, the housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline overall, thereby containing overall inflationary momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labor costs remain weak, they have risen slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4: Different indicators of consumer price inflation; Chart 3.5: Hong Kong's import prices; Chart 3.6: Composite Consumer Price Index, housing rent component, and market rents; Chart 3.7: Unit labor costs. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term due to higher import prices and pandemic-related disruptions to logistics. However, weak rents and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts that overall inflation in 2022 will reach 2.4%, while the government forecasts overall inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022.

Amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalization of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar weakened during the review period. Given ample liquidity in the Hong Kong dollar market, Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) remained low. Overall, foreign exchange and money market transactions in Hong Kong dollars continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions could intensify capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand shocks arising from capital flow fluctuations. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained mostly within the strong side of the Linked Exchange Rate System's convertibility undertaking, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 due to improved market sentiment, its upward momentum subsequently faded, primarily owing to weak net buying by southbound investors through the Stock Connect schemes (Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect) (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, new equity fundraising activities continued to provide support for the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately over the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no indications of abnormal cross-border capital movements. Chart 4.1: Hong Kong dollar exchange rate; Chart 4.2: Net southbound purchases through the Stock Connect schemes; Chart 4.3: Equity funds raised on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK). Although the US dollar strengthened during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable due to the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate index largely followed the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4: Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments, and escalating geopolitical tensions could intensify capital flow volatility. As US interest rates rise, outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds—whose speed and scale will depend on prevailing market conditions—could, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side convertibility undertaking. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, driven primarily by an increase in Exchange Fund Bills (EFBs). Reflecting the continued issuance of EFBs to meet banks' demand for Exchange Fund papers amid ample liquidity in the banking system, EFBs and bonds rose by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before discount window activities) correspondingly fell by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued banknotes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5: Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Bonds. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits increased slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities); thus, it is appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For the full year of 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. Chart 4.6: Deposits of authorized institutions by currency. Overall, interbank market transactions in Hong Kong continued to be smooth and orderly. Given ample liquidity in the banking system, Hong Kong interbank offered rates (HIBOR) remained low despite market concerns about the tightening of US monetary policy (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of rising funding demand toward year-end, HIBOR rose slightly in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages increased modestly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system will provide sufficient buffer against large capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7: Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates. During the review period, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand toward year-end, the overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR in Hong Kong experienced slight volatility in late December 2021, while the 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR in Hong Kong remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8: Overnight and 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, renminbi customer deposits and certificate of deposit (CD) balances grew by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1.1135 trillion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Of this, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, driven mainly by inflows of corporate funds, offsetting a 48.0% decline in CD balances. Chart 4.9: Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six months since July 2021, although renminbi loan balances fell by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. From the end of July 2021 to the end of January 2022, transaction volumes handled by local banks reached RMB 3.763 trillion (Chart 4.10), up 18.3% from RMB 3.181 trillion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's sizable renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payment and financing transactions. For the full year of 2021, the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real-time Gross Settlement System rose to RMB 1.5226 trillion, up from RMB 1.1915 trillion in 2020. Chart 4.10: Renminbi trade settlement and remittances. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the southbound and northbound Stock Connect schemes, Bond Connect, and the Wealth Management Connect; the continued opening of the Mainland capital account; rising demand for renminbi assets from international investors; and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" Initiative and the "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiative. Global major stock markets continued to rally in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have since consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained weak in the fourth quarter of 2021, weighed down primarily by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding the pandemic in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a nearly two-year low in late February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly due to weaker asset market sentiment and a new wave of the pandemic locally. Global major stock markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, driving the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Chart 4.11). Global economic recovery, supported by government monetary and fiscal stimulus, and strong corporate earnings underpinned the rally in global major stock markets, although the pandemic remained investors' primary risk concern throughout the year. However, global major stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022 amid growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies in response to surging inflation risks, sharp rises in commodity prices, and escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag other major global markets at the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index traded between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, value investors' buying interest returned to the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the Hang Seng Index back up to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding the pandemic in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict weighed on the Hang Seng Index, which fell to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points in late February. Over the entire review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11: Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index. Amid the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, equity implied volatility fluctuated sharply in late November 2021 before easing. Although the skew index retreated from its historic high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors' concerns about a correction in the long-term equity rally since the pandemic outbreak and their willingness to allocate more funds to hedge against downside risk in equities (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12: Options implied volatility for the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and the skew index. Against a backdrop of ample global liquidity, Hong Kong stocks have continued to record net inflows of international investor funds since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, the Southbound Stock Connect scheme recorded substantial net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns about the impact of regulatory changes in the Mainland on technology stocks. However, buying through the Southbound Stock Connect scheme began to recover in December 2021, with net inflows totaling HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, cumulative net buying increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13: Net inflows of funds into Hong Kong's stock market; Chart 4.14: Net flows through the stock market connectivity mechanism. After reaching a record high in the first half of 2021, fundraising activity in Hong Kong's primary market slowed in the second half. A total of 98 new listings were recorded in 2021, raising HK$328.9 billion in funds (Chart 4.15), with total funds raised down 17.8% from the previous year. In 2021, the SEHK ranked fourth globally in the IPO market, behind Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15: Hong Kong's initial public offering market. The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. Easing monetary policy in the Mainland and the secondary listing in Hong Kong of more China-concept stocks in the primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding the local pandemic situation, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalization, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Retail banking profitability in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The ratio of non-performing loans rose slightly during this period, but remained low by both historical and international standards. The Hong Kong banking sector remained robust, supported by strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) extended several support measures to further assist the economy in navigating challenging conditions. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to the economic recovery, while the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected will present challenges for banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared to the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was primarily driven by a decline in net interest and non-interest income, coupled with an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets (ROA) fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, down from 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared to 2020, while ROA fell from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1: Retail banking profitability reflects the continued impact of the low interest rate environment; the net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks also remained low at 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2: The NIM of retail banks reflects year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA's issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills, which led to a slight increase in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) in the final quarter of 2021. However, given that liquidity in the banking system remained ample, HIBOR continued to stay at relatively low levels. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks' funding costs remained stable during the review period. In particular, the Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) rose modestly by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3: Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Since June 2019, the Composite Interest Rate has been calculated in accordance with the newly implemented local "Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book" (IRRBB) framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be strictly compared with those from previous months. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong rose slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4: Funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong and US dollars. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local IRRBB framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while those exempted continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost is calculated as a weighted average of the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with those from previous months. Although the normalization of US monetary policy may signal an improvement in banks' profitability, any short-term improvement could be partially offset by two factors. First, although the Federal Reserve has indicated that it will raise interest rates several times in 2022, past experience suggests that changes in local interest rates may lag behind those in the US (especially when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains ample). Consequently, an improvement in banks' net interest margins may take longer to materialize. Additionally, a surge in Omicron cases could introduce uncertainty into the pace of economic recovery, thereby exerting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong and well above international minimum standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.2% at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.5), significantly above the international minimum requirement of 8%. During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio and the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2%, respectively. Furthermore, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions recorded a robust level of 7.9% at the end of 2021, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 3%. Chart 5.5: Capital position of locally incorporated authorized institutions. 1. Consolidated position. 2. Since January 1, 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions have been required to comply with the revised capital adequacy framework, Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards cannot be directly compared with data up to December 2012. In terms of the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained strong during the review period. The average LCR for Category 1 institutions remained high at 151.9% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.6), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Over the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio for Category 2 institutions was 59.1%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.6: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The latest "Net Stable Funding Ratio" (NSFR) also reflects a stable funding position for authorized institutions. The average NSFR for Category 1 institutions remained high at 135.3% in the third quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio for Category 2A institutions also recorded a high level of 150.4%, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75%. The data indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.7: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions. At the end of 2021, customer deposits accounted for 57.6% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level of 57.2% six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8: Liability structure of all authorized institutions. 1. Due to rounding, the sum of the figures may not equal the total. 2. Figures represent percentages of total liabilities (including capital and reserves). 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. In the second half of 2021, total deposits in the banking sector remained largely unchanged, while total loans and advances recorded a slight decline. Consequently, the average loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of the banking sector, expressed in all currencies, fell modestly from 74.1% at the end of June 2021 to 71.8% at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.9). The decline in the LTD ratio was primarily due to a decrease in the foreign currency LTD ratio during the same period, which more than offset the increase in the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio. Reflecting a decrease in foreign currency loans and a corresponding increase in deposits, the average foreign currency LTD ratio fell from 63.3% six months earlier to 57.5% at the end of 2021. In contrast, the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio rose slightly from 84.2% six months earlier to 86.7%, as the decline in Hong Kong dollar deposits exceeded that in Hong Kong dollar loans. Chart 5.9: Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks rose slightly but remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2021. Under a shock assumption of a 200 basis point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks' interest rate positions would amount to 2.53% of their total capital base at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10: Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. 1. The interest rate shock refers to a parallel upward shift of 200 basis points in both the Hong Kong dollar and US dollar yield curves impacting institutions' interest rate risk exposure. At the end of 2021, the majority of locally incorporated licensed banks' interest rate sensitive assets, interest rate sensitive liabilities, and interest rate sensitive off-balance-sheet positions were denominated in Hong Kong dollars or US dollars. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the effect on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the bank's total capital base. 3. Since June 2019, interest rate risk exposure has been calculated in accordance with the newly implemented local "Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book" (IRRBB) framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be strictly compared with those from previous months. Total bank loans decreased in the second half of 2021, largely reflecting a high base effect from new share subscription loans at the end of June. Nevertheless, total loans in the banking sector still recorded an annual growth rate of 3.8% for 2021 as a whole, faster than the 1.2% growth in 2020. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions fell by 3.1% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.11). Excluding new share subscription loans at the end of June 2021, total loans and advances declined slightly by 0.6% during the review period, driven primarily by a modest decrease in local loans (including loans and trade finance used within Hong Kong). Local loans (excluding new share subscription loans in June 2021) contracted by 0.8% in the second half of the year, following strong growth of 5.6% in the first six months. Loans used outside Hong Kong remained largely unchanged from six months earlier. Chart 5.11: Loan growth. The outlook for credit demand is likely to remain stable in the short term. According to the HKMA's "Credit Conditions Survey" conducted in December 2021, the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months increased from 67% six months earlier to 70% (Table 5.A). The overall non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of all authorized institutions rose slightly from 0.86% in June to 0.88% at the end of 2021, while the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans fell slightly from 0.58% to 0.56%. The overall NPL ratio of retail banks increased slightly to 0.83%, and the ratio of past-due and rescheduled loans remained low at 0.50% (Chart 5.12). Despite the slight increase in the NPL ratio, the asset quality of the banking sector remained strong by both historical and international standards. Chart 5.12: Asset quality of retail banks. 1. Non-performing loans refer to loans classified as "substandard," "doubtful," or "loss." 2. Figures prior to December 2015 reflect the situation of retail banks' Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. Since December 2015, the coverage has been extended to include major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks. Household debt grew steadily by 4.4% in both the first and second halves of 2021 (Table 5.B). Within this, private loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2021 to 1.6% in the second half, while residential mortgage loan growth accelerated from 4.0% to 5.7%.

Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impact. In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has dedicated considerable effort to advancing Hong Kong’s climate objectives and enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year’s inclusion of our inaugural Sustainable Development Report as a chapter in the HKMA’s 2021 Annual Report, we are publishing the 2022 Sustainable Development Report as a standalone document for the first time. I hope this report will enable readers to gain a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system’s capacity to address climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling its role as a responsible investor and sustainable institution. Over the past year, we have made significant progress in advancing sustainable development across the HKMA’s core functions. This report outlines our specific measures and initiatives, with key highlights as follows: Banks’ day-to-day operations are exposed to climate risks. As the banking supervisor, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to enhance banks’ ability to address climate change. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to integrate climate risk considerations into our supervisory processes and explored how technology can be leveraged to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. Given the growing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we have also shared best practices with the industry on how to manage these products effectively, thereby strengthening banks’ climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives aimed at addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance. Domestically, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework, which will enhance market transparency and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. Internationally, we are actively engaged with multiple global organizations to help formulate policies for tackling climate change and assess their implications for financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for global bond markets, Hong Kong’s green and sustainable debt issuance continued to grow strongly, increasing by 42% to a total of US$80.5 billion, making it the largest center in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². Notable issuers include the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the Hainan Provincial People’s Government, whose issuances once again demonstrate Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The growth of Hong Kong’s green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds totaling nearly US$16 billion, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We also helped the government achieve two “firsts”: in May 2022, we supported the issuance of the first batch of government green retail bonds, totaling HK$20 billion, which were the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time; and in February 2023, we assisted the government in issuing the first tokenized green bonds. This marked the world’s first issuance of tokenized green bonds by a government and represented a milestone in our successful integration of strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data, and talent are essential elements for fostering a thriving climate finance ecosystem, and their development relies on efforts and collaboration across various sectors. To this end, the HKMA primarily collaborates with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions, and the financial industry—mainly through the Steering Group—to advance these elements. In addition to developing a local green classification framework, as mentioned earlier, the Steering Group has also promoted industry skills training and improved Hong Kong’s data resources through its established Green and Sustainable Finance Center. Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas, such as mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s (HKMA) Exchange Fund’s responsible investment practices, particularly by setting a target for the Exchange Fund portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and long-term risk-adjusted returns. Moreover, to fully capitalize on the opportunities that climate change may present, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment within the Exchange Fund by identifying investment opportunities that support climate transition and mitigation, thereby enhancing the portfolio’s long-term returns. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to 2017 levels. In fact, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to high-carbon assets has consistently remained lower than that of the overall market. Moving forward, we will continue to progress toward our net-zero goal by further integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising our ownership rights, collaborating continuously with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonization and transition. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainable Development Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainable development strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility. In terms of the environment, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and advocating for a more environmentally friendly market to the public; regarding employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive work environment; and in the area of social responsibility, we strive to enhance public financial literacy, promote financial inclusion, and contribute actively to society. Compared to the levels recorded when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage all decreased by double digits in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as a baseline, reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained and collaborative efforts from all parties. On this critical global issue, we recognize the importance of leading by example and working alongside like-minded peers and international organizations. In the following section, we will outline the HKMA’s short-term plans and priorities for addressing climate change across its core functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we are fully committed to meeting this goal. We are confident that, with the collective efforts of our staff, the financial industry, and the public, we will successfully overcome future climate challenges. Chief Executive, Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote sustainable development within Hong Kong’s financial industry and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable organization. At the same time, by participating in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also work to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking sector’s regulator, we will strive to strengthen the banking industry’s climate resilience and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing regulatory requirements for climate risk management, incorporate climate considerations into our supervisory review processes, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking industry’s “green benchmarks.” The HKMA will also support banks in their efforts to enhance climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, quantify, and monitor their climate risk exposure. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regulator-led regular stress testing for the 2023–2024 fiscal year. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risks under an enhanced stress testing framework that covers a range of stress scenarios, including extreme weather events and adverse economic conditions. To foster the sound development of green and sustainable investment products offered by banks, the HKMA will closely monitor local and international market and regulatory developments and maintain communication with the industry to provide timely guidance on sales processes. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the green finance ecosystem and support the financial industry’s green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong’s position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA will assist the government in expanding the issuance of green bonds under the “Government Green Bond Program” and broadening the program’s scope to include sustainable development bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme.” The HKMA will also help implement the government-funded “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. Furthermore, the HKMA will continue to encourage more mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other government departments through the “Cross-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance” on cross-sectoral issues such as skills training and data, green classification taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainable reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Green Banking Alliance, the HKMA will jointly launch various specialized initiatives with the International Finance Corporation in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps for making green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its anchor members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership program to expand the Alliance’s influence in the Asian region. The Alliance will also strengthen efforts to enhance industry professionals’ expertise, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the development of projects in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to global climate action and to implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into its investment management processes, strive toward the net-zero emissions goal, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organization, the HKMA cares about its employees, the wider community, and the surrounding environment. We have developed a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to global carbon reduction and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritize carbon emission reduction and encourage employees to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction efforts. In addition, we will provide further guidance to employees on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To advance digital transformation and increase operational flexibility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernize internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency while minimizing potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change represents a significant risk to the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to the city’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks encounter various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue fulfilling their vital role within the financial system and to channel more funds toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking supervisor, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to address and manage climate risks, and on accelerating banks’ efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and has participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework addresses such risks. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to integrate climate-related factors into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the “Climate Risk Management” module GS-1 of the Supervisory Policy Manual in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges in implementing the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into banking supervision processes and communicated this plan to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of this two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised “Risk-Based Supervisory Approach” module SA-1 of the Supervisory Policy Manual and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by integrating climate risk into risk-based supervisory processes. At the same time, the HKMA refined its climate risk stress testing scenarios and assessment framework based on lessons learned from the 2021 pilot program. The HKMA also plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into regular, supervisor-led stress tests to enable a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year plan, the HKMA is also strengthening its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Concurrently, the HKMA is reviewing its supervisory review process, which is used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. During the review, the HKMA identified a number of good practices and issued a circular in December to share these with the industry, thereby enabling banks to gradually enhance their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks’ ability to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. Additionally, the HKMA, together with other central banks and supervisory authorities, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub to explore how technology solutions can assist in physical risk assessment. The HKMA also places great importance on promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering (AML) practices, employing advanced analytics and compliance technology, supported by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined its AML regulatory data collection process to reduce banks’ manual workload and paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies, the HKMA is collaborating with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. Commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, this framework categorizes economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its associated product is genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has been engaging with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore in depth the characteristics and challenges of the framework, and plans to make recommendations and conduct consultations on its structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognizing that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its current monitoring efforts. In its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and supervisory authorities to gain a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022, focusing on two key topics: greenwashing in the corporate green bond market3 and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposure4. The findings of these studies help inform policy and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Domestically, these studies contribute to strengthening the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research seminars and its own “Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report.” The HKMA’s Liquidity Facility Framework is a collateralized standby liquidity arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is exploring the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through this engagement, the HKMA helps foster policy dialogue among international and regional stakeholders on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws insights to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has intensified its efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide essential infrastructure and incentives, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial industry’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the government’s climate strategy¹. The Steering Group’s work is guided primarily by its strategic plan, which outlines six key focus areas and five action agendas to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). These include: enhancing climate-related financial risk management to solidify Hong Kong’s status as a global risk management center; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation, and investor protection; improving relevant skills among industry professionals and raising public awareness; encouraging product innovation and research to channel funds toward green and sustainable projects; capitalizing on opportunities presented by the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance center for the Guangdong‑Hong Kong‑Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. To date, the Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment in advancing sustainable finance development in Hong Kong. Its current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Green and Sustainable Finance Center (see below), a green taxonomy (see “Establishing a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Capital Flows” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainable reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities in Hong Kong in March and will support Hong Kong’s development as a regional carbon trading hub, including the development of an international high‑quality voluntary carbon market and the leveraging of opportunities arising from Greater Bay Area cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP² to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of this collaboration, both parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting private companies and small and medium‑sized enterprises (SMEs). This facilitates sustainability reporting for companies while helping financial institutions collect and analyze company‑level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks an important step in expanding the Steering Group’s data initiatives to include SMEs, a previously hard‑to‑reach yet vital segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Green and Sustainable Finance Center in July 2021 to coordinate training and policy development efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and academic institutions, and to build up resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Center launched three knowledge hubs focusing on data, training information, and internship opportunities, respectively, to help the financial industry and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The knowledge hub provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong and supports industry talent development; accordingly, the Center assisted the government in launching the “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” in December, offering subsidies to practitioners, students, and graduates participating in relevant training and skills enhancement programs. Other measures to promote skills training include the launch of the “Sustainable Finance Internship Scheme” to create more internship opportunities for students, and the development of a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the HKMA’s “Banking Professional Qualification Framework” for banking practitioners. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance”⁴, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry organizations, research institutions, and providers of innovative technology to create a collaborative platform for developing green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realize their potential in making green finance a mainstream core business and to promote the financial system’s participation in global climate‑change‑related activities. It operates by providing financial institutions with a one‑stop platform for mutual learning, where they can access the knowledge, tools, and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; it also convenes green finance leaders, connects green financial institutions across different emerging markets, facilitates communication and exploration of cutting‑edge issues, and advances the global green finance agenda, unlocking limitless green and climate‑related investment opportunities. In June, five globally leading financial institutions⁵ became cornerstone members of the Alliance and have been working closely with the IFC and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities that contribute to the green economic transition. Additionally, three global partners and one knowledge partner⁶ committed in 2022 to provide climate expertise in areas such as innovation, standardization, and academic research. Details of the Alliance and its member structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone Members, IFC, and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding. Meanwhile, since March 2021, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtable discussions, attracting more than 6,000 participants from across the globe, including the Asia‑Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. Furthermore, in June 2022, the Alliance jointly published its first cutting‑edge research report, titled “Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices, and Regulation,” with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)⁷. The HKMA has consistently promoted the issuance of green and sustainable debt and cultivated a local ecosystem of related professional services. In 2022, total green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong (including bonds and loans) reached US$80.5 billion, representing a 42% increase. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the government’s commitment to addressing climate change, advancing green finance, and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the government launched the “Government Green Bond Program” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of related green bond issuances. To date, the government has issued green institutional and retail bonds totaling nearly US$16 billion, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability under the program, the government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report” detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable citizens to participate in Hong Kong’s sustainable development and share its benefits through investment, the first batch of green retail bonds, totaling HK$20 billion, was issued in May and received strong public support, becoming the largest green retail bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance also expanded the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, reinforcing its position as a leading green finance hub regionally and internationally. The government continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds in the 2022‑23 fiscal year, issuing green bonds equivalent to US$5.75 billion in January 2023. This three‑currency issuance covered the US dollar, euro, and renminbi, with maturities ranging from two to 30 years, continuing to provide an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in previous government green bond issuances, reflecting investors’ confidence in Hong Kong’s long‑term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bond to RMB10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating through the “Southbound” link of Bond Connect also increased, showcasing Hong Kong’s role as a leading offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its position as an international financial center. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the government in issuing tokenized institutional green bonds to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This marked the first issuance of tokenized green bonds by a government worldwide. This primary issuance was settled on a private blockchain network on a T+1 basis, and subsequent processes—including coupon payments, secondary market trade settlement, and redemption at maturity—were also digitized. The experience gained from this government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in similar bond issuances in the future. To provide credible and convenient market information to the industry, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) to publish annual reports on Hong Kong’s and the region’s green debt markets. The ICMA report shows that in 2022, Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds, with a total issuance volume of US$27.8 billion arranged through Hong Kong, accounting for more than one‑third of the regional total. Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bonds: US$27.8 billion. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB5 billion offshore local government bond in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion in green and blue bonds⁸. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also issued its first offshore bond in Hong Kong, totaling RMB5 billion, comprising blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances repeatedly highlight Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as the region’s premier fundraising platform. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme,” launched in 2021, and leverages the scheme to attract more providers of related professional services—including financial institutions, green consultancy firms, and external reviewers—to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The scheme has been well received by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the scheme had covered expenses for external review services incurred before, after, or both before and after issuance for more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. Starting in March, the scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan threshold for applying for external review cost subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, making it easier for smaller enterprises to access green financing. Following the successful completion of a proof‑of‑concept for tokenized retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA again collaborated with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalized carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity, and environmental integrity of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver, and transfer digitalized MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) plays a pivotal role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment; as early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles for Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission and to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, with long-term value creation," believing that consideration of ESG factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate associated risks.
