In response to the increasingly severe challenges posed by climate change, the HKMA continues to advance its responsible investment journey, including setting a "net-zero emissions by 2050" target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategies to improve the resilience of its asset portfolio, thereby delivering better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, collaborating with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment and working with international organizations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information is critical to managing climate risks. To fulfill its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) of central banks and supervisors at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in line with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term; b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment; c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System; d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes a responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to prioritize ESG investments that offer risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to those of other investments, thereby aligning with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website. The Investment Committee, which operates under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management policies, and monitors progress in integrating ESG factors and the Exchange Fund’s ESG status through regular reports from the Risk Management and Oversight Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As illustrated in Figure 1, the ESG Committee, established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office and chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing all ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The ESG Committee reports the motions discussed and progress made at each meeting to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Governance and oversight structure for responsible investment: A dedicated team within the Risk Management and Oversight Division works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investments: For public market investments, the Credit, Regulatory, and Oversight Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed-income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Oversight Division. Additionally, the Risk Management and Oversight Division participates in the selection, appointment, and monitoring of external investment managers for the equity portfolio from an ESG perspective (see the section "Striving to Actively Exercise Ownership of Assets" under "Risk Management" on page 27 for details). For private market investments, the Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal provided by the Risk Management and Oversight Division and the private market investment team. Concrete evidence² continues to demonstrate that the impact of climate change and related risks is significant. According to the latest report³ from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even if the "nationally determined contributions" announced by all regions are fully implemented, global temperatures are projected to rise by 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close this temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴, along with market-driven asset repricing based on expected future trends and inherent physical risks, will intensify pressure on asset valuations. Given updates to global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA, leveraging the expertise of external consultants, has further assessed the resilience of the Exchange Fund’s "portfolio" under a "rapid transition" scenario (Figure 2), in addition to the scenarios previously evaluated in 2021. The "rapid transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium, and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments together drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets face sudden divestment to keep the average temperature increase below 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2100. This scenario largely aligns with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "portfolio" remains robust in the medium to long term, as a larger proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Industry distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may cause short-term performance shocks, particularly for equity assets. The "portfolio" as a whole will be increasingly affected by physical risks that become more pronounced over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Climate scenario analysis, like other model-based approaches, has its limitations. The analysis is based on market benchmark industry distributions at the strategic asset allocation level and does not consider the effect of actively selecting specific securities within an industry. More in-depth research shows that investments within the "portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or less affected compared to the market benchmark of strategic asset allocation. This result reaffirms that the HKMA’s responsible investment approach, focused on combating climate change, enhances portfolio resilience. Climate change trajectories remain uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review relevant scenarios and refine its assessments to more clearly identify the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully recognizes the risks and opportunities that climate change can present. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities related to climate transition, climate risk mitigation, and enhancing long-term portfolio returns. In 2022, the HKMA continued its strong momentum, increasing its holdings of green, social, and sustainable bonds by another 50%. For equity investments, the HKMA invests in an actively managed equity portfolio focused on governance themes and adopts a decarbonization strategy for its passive equity portfolio that favors companies with low carbon emissions. Additionally, the HKMA is exploring the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio with dedicated partners of the Exchange Fund’s "Long-term Growth Portfolio" to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Figure 3). Figure 3: Continued implementation of measures to increase ESG investment. The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator that, in addition to producing clean energy, places great emphasis on social and biodiversity considerations. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poison bait to prevent predators from attacking their livestock, but this inadvertently harmed vultures, some of which are endangered species. Livestock is a vital asset for local villagers, and to help villagers protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to safeguard animals from natural predators. Additionally, the operator employs a bird monitoring team to issue warnings when vultures are attracted to animal carcasses left behind by predators, prompting the shutdown of wind turbines to prevent vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win situation: it secures villagers’ livelihoods while also reducing vulture fatalities caused by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Strong ESG practices can create additional business opportunities and revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operation. The investee company is a comprehensive logistics and warehousing operator in mainland China, specializing in cold-chain logistics for pharmaceuticals, chemical products, and high-end consumer goods. The company faces rising ESG operational standards, primarily driven by multinational corporate clients requiring their service providers to meet high decarbonization targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to this demand, the company engaged external consultants to help develop a "three-year ESG plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonization plan already yielded significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures earned the company the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and accolades have enabled the company to secure numerous business opportunities from multinational corporate clients in the consumer and chemical sectors, who place particular emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully hosted its 4th annual ESG workshop, engaging with nine participating private market institutions (including general partners, limited partners, and corporates) to share best ESG practices and promote sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public market, the HKMA has urged trading partners, primarily investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr. Li Dah-chi, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered the opening remarks at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop. At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in developing industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the first central banks to sign up to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a collaborative effort among PRI signatories to develop a unified responsible investment due diligence questionnaire⁵,⁶ for private equity and venture capital investments, aimed at assisting private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in several working groups to support FCLTGlobal’s research, which explores key market practices for long-term portfolio construction and decarbonization of private assets, as well as the application of these practices to long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS’s "Central Bank Climate-related Disclosure Guidance" to demonstrate its commitment to adopting sound ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a working group under the NGFS’s "Central Bank Net-Zero Emissions" working group, participating in the development of sustainable and responsible investment guidelines for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. Liu Hui-chuan, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (center), speaking at an ESG investment opportunity sharing session. Building internal capabilities is essential for continuing to advance the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging employees to take relevant sustainability courses and obtain related qualifications, the HKMA has also drawn knowledge and practical experience from the process in 2021 whereby external consultants provided advice on key industry practices for portfolio climate transition. On the other hand, the HKMA utilizes ESG data compiled by reputable external data providers to complement its ongoing portfolio analysis, thereby helping to strengthen the Exchange Fund’s ESG resilience.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own carbon footprint, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s overall climate objectives. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also upholds its commitments to employee well‑being, financial inclusion, and social responsibility. The HKMA is dedicated to conducting its day‑to‑day operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, it pursues sustainability under three pillars—environment, employees, and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee leads the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives and representatives from the Risk Management and Supervision Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department; it submits regular reports to the Governance Committee of the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the committee’s leadership, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and executing measures within their respective domains. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved climate targets for the HKMA’s operations and reviewed the roadmap for achieving net‑zero emissions by 2050 or sooner. During the year, the committee continued to assess progress on the HKMA’s green initiatives, including recommendations to strengthen its sustainable procurement policies, procedures, and methods. Governance framework for sustainability: In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, employees, and society at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service presented the HKMA with the “15 Years+ Caring Heart” logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to its own carbon footprint and has established an internal Green Office Guide to manage the environmental impact of its operational processes. Environmental considerations have been integrated into the interior design, operation, and maintenance of the HKMA’s offices. In 2022, the HKMA was awarded the Gold rating under the BEAM Plus (Interior) 1.0 scheme for certain renovated office areas. This marks the second green building certification received, following the LEED Gold certification awarded in 2021. Having obtained the Gold rating under BEAM Plus (Interior) 1.0, the HKMA has implemented various energy‑saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per employee), a 24.4% decrease compared with 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 2022 amounted to 2,996.4 tCO2e (1.7 tCO2e per employee), a 38.2% reduction from 2015 (Figure 2). Figure 1; Figure 2: GHG emission intensity (Scope 1 and 2). The HKMA encourages paperless operations within the organization. In addition, it has implemented a print management system that requires employees to log in to printers to confirm each print request, thereby helping to reduce unnecessary printing and toner consumption. When printing is essential, double‑sided printing and black‑and‑white output are encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic record‑keeping system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per employee), a 65.3% decrease from 2015 (Figure A). Figure A: Paper intensity. The HKMA’s waste management continues to follow the “4R” principle (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover). In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA has reduced electronic waste by adopting technology solutions such as server virtualization and private‑cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit, analyzing the composition of waste generated in its offices. The audit revealed that food waste accounted for a significant portion of total waste, prompting the HKMA to launch a food‑waste recycling program (see page 41, “Enhancing Waste Management”). Total non‑hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general refuse and recyclable waste) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per employee), a 4.8% decrease from 2015 (Figure 3). Fluctuations were mainly due to work‑from‑home arrangements during the peak of the COVID‑19 pandemic and the subsequent resumption of office operations after the fifth wave. Figure 3: Non‑hazardous waste intensity. The HKMA prioritizes waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing, and recycling materials. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit, to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste (plastics, paper, metal, glass, wood, electronics, etc.) generated in daily operations and to provide recommendations for waste reduction. Based on the audit results, the HKMA launched a food‑waste recycling program in November, installing food‑waste collection bins in all tea rooms. Food waste collected daily is transported to an organic resources recovery center in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy for electricity generation. Residual materials from the conversion process can also be made into compost for landscaping and agricultural use. In addition, recycling bins are conveniently located throughout the office. The HKMA shares recycling tips with employees and places greater emphasis on further improving source separation of recyclables, as well as on handling instructions for recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles. Moreover, we continue to organize activities to raise employees’ environmental awareness, explain waste‑management policies, and encourage the use of office recycling facilities. Food waste collected daily is sent to an organic resources recovery center; plastic items are recycled. The HKMA operates two data centers (one for production and one for backup). Since they account for a major portion of the organization’s overall energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green design and various energy‑saving measures, including rack‑level air‑conditioning systems, LED lighting, and 24‑hour monitoring of energy performance. Following the completion of a consultancy study in 2022 on the green performance of these data centers, the HKMA is preparing to implement recommendations to improve overall energy efficiency. It has also begun preparations for obtaining green data‑center certification. Recognizing the importance of building a sustainability culture, the HKMA regularly introduces various programs and activities to educate and encourage employees to adopt habits that support sustainability and to embrace green and digital work practices. The HKMA shares green‑living tips with employees, as well as annual office‑wide energy and paper consumption statistics, to remind them to contribute to environmental efforts at the individual level; it also encourages employees to submit suggestions on sustainability matters. Led by a Senior Manager of the Administrative Group, a task force brings together employees from different departments to brainstorm ideas and concrete measures for promoting a green work environment. Members of the task force also serve as ambassadors when new green initiatives are launched. The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt more environmentally friendly operational practices and has introduced various measures to improve operational efficiency at the HKMA, within the financial industry, and across the economy, thereby minimizing resource consumption. The HKMA’s “Submission of Returns Electronically through Transmission (STET) System” is a one‑stop platform that enables banks to submit documents to the HKMA electronically, covering a range of periodic returns required on a weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annual basis. Another system, the “e‑Delivery System,” is a secure electronic communication channel through which the HKMA issues notices, guidelines, and other information to banks. Both systems help save significant amounts of paper each year. In handling bank complaints and enforcement work, the HKMA has taken steps to support paperless submission of documents; bank customers can lodge complaints through electronic channels and by completing online forms. The HKMA is also developing a next‑generation management information system to facilitate complaint handling and the transition from paper‑based to digital records. To reduce paper usage, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) has adopted digital signatures in its day‑to‑day communications with participants, including the issuance of notices, account opening and termination letters, and responses to audit confirmations. Looking ahead, the CMU will continue to explore additional green measures, including the adoption of automated electronic processes for internal and external communications. By promoting the use of the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored value facilities (SVFs), the HKMA encourages the public to adopt electronic payment methods more widely, as alternatives to cash and physical cheques. Further information on FPS and SVFs is provided in the chapter “Hong Kong’s Position as an International Financial Centre” of the HKMA’s 2022 Annual Report. Distributing electronic red packets (e‑red packets) is simple and convenient, and helps reduce the use of physical red envelopes and banknotes, thereby supporting Hong Kong’s sustainable development. To this end, the HKMA continues to actively promote e‑red packets through various social media and traditional platforms, encouraging the public to use FPS or other e‑wallet services via online or mobile banking to distribute e‑red packets during the Lunar New Year. Major banks and e‑wallet operators have also organized various activities to encourage users to adopt e‑red packets, such as providing festive user interfaces, enhancing functionality for greater convenience, and offering lucky draws or cash rebates. The HKMA’s promotion of e‑red packets on social media: For members of the public who choose to distribute physical red packets during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA continues to encourage the use of “new‑year notes”—clean, crisp banknotes—to serve as red‑packet envelopes. Using new‑year notes reduces the need to print new banknotes, thereby lessening environmental impact. Feedback from note‑issuing banks indicates that the public has become increasingly receptive to new‑year notes in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts to promote the recycling of coins. Coins collected through the programme are returned to circulation to meet public demand, enhancing the efficiency of coin circulation and reducing the need for minting. The programme operates two coin‑collection vehicles that have served more than one million people to date, collecting over 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HK$1.3 billion. In 2022, about 78% of users chose to use some or all of the coins they exchanged to top up their SVF accounts. The HKMA has maintained its collaboration with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, deploying coin‑collection vehicles on NGO Flag Day to collect coins and support social services. Coin‑counting machines on the vehicles: The Coin Collection Programme, launched in 2014, is the world’s first systematic coin‑collection programme using a mobile‑vehicle concept. It has received numerous local and international awards over the years, with its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin handling widely recognized. The programme operates two coin‑collection vehicles, each equipped with two high‑speed coin‑counting machines to collect coins exchanged by the public. Members of the public can choose to exchange their coins for banknotes, use them to top up SVF accounts (such as Octopus cards or e‑wallets), or donate them to the Community Chest for charitable purposes. In addition to collecting coins, the vehicles are also occasionally deployed for various educational activities, such as student visits.

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency (HKQAA) has conducted an independent verification of the climate targets (the "Climate Targets") of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (the "HKMA"). The Climate Targets were established with reference to the requirements set forth in the SBTi Corporate Manual (the "SBTi Corporate Manual"). The purpose of this verification is to confirm that the Climate Targets were developed in accordance with the SBTi Corporate Manual. This verification was performed in accordance with the "International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised): Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information," issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to enable the expression of an opinion and a conclusion, thereby providing a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in line with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and presentation of the data. Our verification work is conducted with complete independence and impartiality. Based on the results of this verification, HKQAA provides reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. Sheung Siu-Yin, Audit Manager, HKQAA, March 2023. Verification Statement: HKQAA has conducted an independent verification of the 2022 environmental data (the "2022 Data") of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (the "HKMA"). The 2022 Data include total energy consumption, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission intensity, paper consumption intensity, and the intensity and recycling rate of non-hazardous waste generated for 2022, as well as the changes in these metrics compared to 2015 levels. The HKMA's GHG emissions data were compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (the "GHG Protocol"), jointly published by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD). The scope of verification covers the relevant data for the period from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2022, as well as the relevant data for the period from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2015, used for annual performance comparison. The verification scope encompasses a total of six office and warehouse assets: four offices—1) International Finance Centre Phase II Office, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) Taikoo Place Phase I, and 4) Kowloon Trade Centre; and two warehouses—5) Lok Shing Industrial Centre and 6) Cheung Lee Centre, located in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan, respectively. The purpose of the verification is to provide reasonable assurance regarding the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA's data collection mechanisms. Within the verification scope, HKQAA reviewed representative data and supporting evidence selected from the six assets. This verification was performed in accordance with the "International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised): Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information," issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to enable the expression of an opinion and a conclusion, thereby providing a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in line with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tested the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing selected sample data back to their sources, and it also reviewed the underlying procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checks, performing reliability tests where appropriate. The verification process further included an assessment of internal data collection and management mechanisms, interviews with representatives responsible for preparing the 2022 Data, and the selection of representative data and information for examination. Relevant raw data and supporting evidence were also subject to detailed review during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and presentation of the data. Our verification work is conducted with complete independence and impartiality. The HKQAA verification team was not involved in the preparation of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, HKQAA provides reasonable assurance regarding the 2022 Data and concludes that: • The 2022 Data are materially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA's overall data collection mechanisms are adequate. Sheung Siu-Yin, Audit Manager, HKQAA, March 2023.

Scaling up and accelerating climate action has become the most pressing challenge of our time. Nearly half of the critical decade for tackling the climate crisis has already passed. To have any chance of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, we need to cut global carbon emissions by more than 40% during this decade. Yet greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach record highs. The latest climate science indicates that the window of opportunity to keep global temperature increases within 1.5 degrees Celsius is rapidly closing. The effects of a 1.1-degree Celsius rise in temperature are already evident to all—record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding, and storms are occurring more frequently and with greater intensity around the world. Hong Kong is no exception; last September, after being hit by a powerful super typhoon, we were immediately confronted with a once-in-a-century rainstorm. Despite our robust infrastructure and rapid disaster response capabilities, the impact was still severe—widespread flooding, transport disruptions, and damage to numerous roads. All of this serves as a stark reminder that decisive and proactive climate action is urgently needed. Asia faces particularly significant challenges on the path to low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that can appropriately balance climate action with economic growth and social inclusion. This is no easy task. Given the region’s rapid economic development and fast-growing population, its carbon emissions account for more than half of the global total. At the same time, the Asia-Pacific region’s high population density and geographical location make it vulnerable to rising sea levels and extreme weather events. Because economies in the region are at different stages of development, while low-carbon transition will create new opportunities for some economies, for others, raising the necessary transition funding will be a major challenge. Market estimates suggest that the Asia-Pacific region will require more than US$3 trillion in low-carbon transition investment annually over the next 30 years. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong has both the capacity and the responsibility to harness the power of finance to support low-carbon transition across Asia. As a banking regulator, market facilitator, and responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been making significant efforts to advance the sustainability agenda. Readers can learn about the various concrete measures and initiatives the HKMA has introduced over the past year from the different chapters of this report. In addition, to strengthen the HKMA’s internal governance structure and coordinate sustainability work across different functional areas more effectively, we established the Green and Sustainable Finance Steering Group last year. For details on this steering group, please refer to the newly added chapter on “Governance of Sustainable Development.” Hong Kong banks play a vital role in supporting Asia’s transition to net-zero emissions. In addition to fulfilling our traditional role as a banking regulator by ensuring that banks properly manage climate risks in our day-to-day supervision, we also act as a facilitator, supporting the banking industry in providing financing for the low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green classification framework to help banks and other financial institutions identify environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate goals. We launched a prototype of the green classification framework for consultation in May and are now refining it based on feedback received during the consultation period. Furthermore, as demand grows for higher-quality and more globally comparable sustainable disclosure information, the HKMA is working with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board in June—a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator is not limited to developing frameworks and rules; we are also committed to addressing pain points faced by the industry. Currently, many banks struggle to conduct physical risk assessments due to data limitations. In response, the HKMA will soon launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform that will enable banks to assess the impact of physical hazards on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios simply by entering a property address, thereby helping banks manage related climate risks. As a major international financial centre and sustainable finance hub in Asia, Hong Kong has long served as a bridge, channelling international investment into sustainable development projects in Asia to support the region’s low-carbon transition. In recent years, the total amount of international green and sustainable bonds issued in Hong Kong has accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, significantly outpacing other regions. Notably, the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong for the third and second consecutive years, respectively, in 2023, reaffirming Hong Kong’s important role as a green gateway linking the mainland with the rest of the world. The vibrancy of Hong Kong’s sustainable bond market is partly due to the demonstration effect of the “Government Green Bond Programme.” Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds totalling approximately US$25 billion to institutional and retail investors. We have used each issuance as an opportunity to innovate and expand the features of green bonds, including currency, tenor, and distribution channels, thereby setting a foundation for other public and private green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bond in 2022, we issued the world’s first tokenized government green bonds in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the issuance of a second batch of tokenized green bonds; these bonds were denominated in four major currencies and issued in digital-native form, making them the world’s first multi-currency digital green bonds. At the same time, we have proactively introduced various measures to enhance the vibrancy and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem. This includes work in areas such as skills training, data improvement, green fintech, and transition finance. In particular, with regard to talent development, we launched a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Banking Professional Qualification Framework in 2023 to provide banking professionals with a systematic curriculum to enhance their understanding and expertise in green and sustainable finance. Transition finance is another key area of focus for us; it provides funding for decarbonisation activities in high-emission and hard-to-abate industries, preventing these industries from failing to transition due to a lack of financial support. To support the sound development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand Hong Kong’s green classification framework to cover transition activities. We will also expand the scope of the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme,” which provides subsidies to eligible bond issuers and borrowers, to include transition bonds and loans, thereby encouraging companies in the region to raise transition funds in Hong Kong. In addition, we will strengthen communication and engagement with relevant stakeholders to attract private sector investment in sustainable development projects that have previously struggled to secure financing through public-private partnerships and blended finance models. Some of the above work requires cross-sector collaboration and is primarily coordinated by the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional cooperation is equally important. In addition to our long-term partnership with the International Finance Corporation on the “Green Business Banking Alliance,” the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office also joined the “Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance” and the “Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership” as a founding member in 2023. Furthermore, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero announced plans to establish a branch in Hong Kong. Through these partnerships, we hope to promote skills training and knowledge sharing, thereby supporting the channelling of funds to sustainable development projects in the region and around the world. To promote new business development and knowledge exchange, the HKMA also helped organise the first “Hong Kong Green Week” earlier this year, attracting more than 1,600 participants from nearly 30 regions, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial sectors, to discuss solutions for expanding climate finance in the region and to forge new partnerships. Mr. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive of the HKMA, delivered a speech at the “APAC Climate Business Forum,” a flagship event of “Hong Kong Green Week.” As the manager of Hong Kong’s official reserves and a major global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of investing in green and sustainable assets and has gradually expanded the ESG and green asset portfolio of the Exchange Fund in both public and private markets. In line with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s “portfolio” by 2050 or earlier, the HKMA added a new actively managed global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition last year, while expanding the application of a customised low-carbon stock index to another public market asset portfolio. In addition, green, social, and sustainability bonds, which the HKMA prioritises for investment, have outperformed investment benchmarks, demonstrating the principle of “doing well by doing good.” In private markets, we continue to pursue green-related investment opportunities and have become an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. As of the end of 2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 6% and 46% compared to 2021 and 2017 levels, respectively, and has consistently remained below the overall market level. As a sustainable organisation, the HKMA will continue to strive for improvement, setting our sustainability goals and plans based on the three pillars of environment, employees, and social responsibility. Specifically, in our low-carbon transition journey, the HKMA is continuously strengthening our ability to address climate change by assessing our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures cover emissions reduction, energy efficiency improvement, and waste management, with the ultimate goal of achieving our commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We have already developed plans to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions in the short term and are making good progress towards our medium-term goal of reducing Scope 2 emissions by 2030. In addition to green targets, the HKMA is also committed to promoting the physical and mental well-being of employees in order to attract and retain top talent to fulfil the HKMA’s various important functions. Furthermore, by working with various stakeholders, we contribute to creating a caring society by promoting financial inclusion, enhancing citizens’ financial literacy, and raising public awareness of financial fraud prevention. The climate challenge is enormous and extremely urgent. Economies around the world are moving towards a more sustainable future, a process that is expected to bring about significant changes in financing activities and asset allocation. This transformation carries considerable risks, but it will also bring unprecedented opportunities. As a leading global sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has a responsibility to take the lead in addressing these challenges. At the same time, we are well positioned to seize the opportunity. The HKMA will fully support the industry in providing financing for the low-carbon transition; continue to lead by example as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation; and work with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

Climate change risks and other sustainability issues are global concerns. The HKMA’s objective in its sustainability efforts is to play a leading role through its own policies and operations, ensuring that both Hong Kong’s financial system and the HKMA itself are resilient to climate change risks and can support the transition to a more sustainable economy. By actively participating in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also strive to contribute to the development of green and sustainable finance policies and standards at the regional and global levels. As the banking sector’s regulator, the HKMA will further strengthen banks’ climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. Specifically, key priorities include: conducting a new round of thematic reviews of banks’ climate risk management practices and holding a new series of consultation meetings as part of the assessment of banks’ progress in implementing climate risk management regulatory requirements; continuing work to integrate climate considerations into the HKMA’s supervisory review process; completing a second round of industry-wide climate risk stress tests, providing guidance to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing observations and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures, including collaborating with relevant local authorities to align relevant requirements with the International Financial Reporting Standards’ Sustainability Disclosure Standards—which serve as a global benchmark—and preparing for the implementation of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s Third Pillar framework for climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidance on best practices for transition planning with the industry. To promote the sound development of green and sustainable investment products offered by banks, the HKMA will continue to monitor local and international market and regulatory developments and maintain close communication with the industry to ensure that banks adopt appropriate sales procedures. In addition, the HKMA will also act as a facilitator, committed to fostering the development of a green finance ecosystem and supporting banks in financing the economic transition. We will soon publish a local green taxonomy and continue to expand its coverage to include more activities, such as transition activities. At the same time, we will continue to explore the application of technology solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposure; one example is a cloud platform to be launched soon, which will facilitate banks’ physical risk assessments. To enhance professionals’ expertise, we will also develop a professional-level module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the “Banking Professional Qualification Framework” in 2024. Hong Kong is well-positioned to serve as a regional and international hub for sustainable finance. To fulfill this role, the HKMA is assisting the government in implementing the recommendations of the 2023–24 Budget to expand the scope of the “Government Green Bond Programme” to include sustainable finance projects, thereby deepening the development of the local green and sustainable bond market; at the same time, it is attracting more green financing activities, including transition finance activities, to Hong Kong through the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme.” We will also continue to encourage more governments, institutions, and enterprises to raise green funds through Hong Kong and explore potential synergies between green finance and technology. Furthermore, we will continue to support the implementation of the government-funded “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. As co-chair of the “Cross-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance” (the Steering Group), we will continue to work closely with other government departments to coordinate cross-sectoral policies and initiatives aimed at promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In 2024, the Steering Group will focus its efforts on three areas: sustainable disclosure, the application of technology, and transition finance. As another key focus, through the “Green Banking Alliance,” the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will continue to jointly launch various specialized initiatives in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks support financial institutions in establishing their own tailored green transition pathways. In 2024, we will also strive to deepen our cooperation with the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, the Capacity Building Coalition for Sustainable Investment, and the Partnership for Green Development Investment and Financing. As a responsible investor, the HKMA is committed to achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s portfolio by 2050 or sooner. We will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments through a three-pronged approach to responsible investment, ensuring portfolio resilience throughout the journey to net zero. We recognize that achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement requires a transition across the entire economy; therefore, we are optimizing our net-zero strategy to focus on assets that can deliver positive climate benefits to the real economy, while balancing the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. As an organization committed to environmental protection, the HKMA’s decarbonization strategy will continue to evolve to reflect the latest developments in markets, regulations, technology, and other climate-related areas. To further strengthen the HKMA’s climate resilience and risk preparedness, we will explore the feasibility of using technology solutions to assess the impact of physical risks on our offices. In addition, we will continue to actively encourage employees to participate in our sustainability efforts, including launching campaigns to foster sustainable habits and optimizing office processes and practices. Furthermore, the HKMA will continue to maintain a consistent, efficient, and sustainable procurement approach, including assessing suppliers’ ESG practices when selecting and renewing contracts. Building on the Green Data Center certification obtained in 2023, the HKMA is committed to adhering to the specified certification standards. For periodic updates to data center facilities, in addition to keeping pace with the latest technological developments, we will also incorporate green design and operational practices. At the same time, we will continue to reduce electronic waste through the application of technology and convergence, and actively modernize internal systems to improve efficiency and minimize potential risks as much as possible. Finally, in the area of social focus, the HKMA will identify more community service opportunities for its staff and work with the industry to promote financial inclusion and improve financial literacy, as well as raise public awareness of fraud prevention.

Climate change affects every aspect of human life, and everyone can contribute to mitigating its impact. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) contributes to promoting and accelerating the transition to net-zero emissions in Hong Kong and across Asia through its multiple roles as a central banking institution, banking supervisor, market facilitator, responsible investor, and sustainability-focused organization. The HKMA has established a robust sustainable development governance framework to lead the formulation of its related strategies and policies, oversee the implementation of relevant measures, and ensure that sustainability considerations are integrated into its own operations and business practices. To uphold good corporate governance, the HKMA has developed a sound sustainable development governance structure with clear accountability arrangements and high transparency for its sustainability-related work. This governance framework ensures that sustainability considerations are effectively integrated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, and provides effective mechanisms to monitor and assess the progress and effectiveness of its sustainability initiatives. The HKMA’s sustainable development governance framework comprises: the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant sub-committees, which monitor the HKMA’s work—including its sustainability efforts—and make recommendations; the Green and Sustainable Finance Steering Committee (the Steering Committee), chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, which leads the HKMA’s overall environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategy and policies at the management level; with regard to responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, which coordinates and oversees ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office; and for other functional areas, relevant teams and working groups that plan and implement sustainability measures related to banking and market development, as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (the Steering Group), co-established by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the efforts of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and other stakeholders to accelerate the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. Given the significant expansion of the HKMA’s sustainability initiatives over the past few years, we established the Steering Committee in October as a new central platform to lead and coordinate more effectively all sustainability work across the HKMA’s various functional areas.1 It provides guidance on the formulation of strategies, policies, and plans for ESG-related matters across four functional areas—banking, market development, Exchange Fund investment, and internal operations; oversees the implementation of ESG-related initiatives by the HKMA’s functional departments; assesses the HKMA’s performance and effectiveness in achieving its ESG objectives; and oversees external communication strategies. The Steering Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with three Deputy Chief Executives serving as permanent members. Additionally, we invite Assistant Chief Executives responsible for key functions related to green and sustainable finance to attend Steering Committee meetings to report on key outcomes and future plans of their respective work. The Steering Committee meets regularly and is supported by relevant working groups from the HKMA’s Banking Department, the Infrastructure, Development and Operations Division, the External Department, and the Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition to developing and implementing its own sustainability measures, the HKMA co-established the Steering Group with the SFC in May 2020.2 As a cross-agency platform, the Steering Group provides strategic direction and coordinates cross-sectoral efforts to address climate and environmental risks in the financial industry, thereby strengthening Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub in Asia and globally. For details on the work of the Steering Group, please refer to the chapter “Strengthening the Green and Sustainable Finance Ecosystem.”

Climate change poses a significant risk to the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks encounter various sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue fulfilling their vital role in the financial system and channel more funds toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to address and manage climate risks, and on accelerating banks’ efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA is committed to developing various policy measures to enhance the banking system’s ability to cope with climate risks. In August, the HKMA issued a circular on net-zero transition planning, setting out high-level principles to help banks remain safe and sound during the economy’s transition to net-zero emissions. Following the issuance of that circular, we conducted a survey in the fourth quarter among a sample of banks to understand their transition planning measures. Based on the survey results, we will share observations and best practices on transition planning with the industry and will organize seminars or workshops to facilitate experience sharing among industry participants. Regarding disclosure requirements, in light of recent international developments—including the International Sustainability Standards Board’s (ISSB) International Financial Reporting Sustainability Disclosure Standards announced in June, and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s (BCBS) November consultation on a third-pillar disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks—the HKMA is intensifying its efforts to enhance the sustainability-related disclosure framework for Hong Kong banks. Specifically, the HKMA is working with local authorities and stakeholders to develop a comprehensive roadmap for Hong Kong that aligns with the ISSB standards. During the year, the HKMA stepped up its supervision of banks’ climate risk management and provided guidance to banks to help them further strengthen their climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA has made significant progress in implementing a two-year plan to integrate climate risk considerations into banking supervision. Climate risk management is now a standing agenda item for prudential supervisory meetings held with bank management. Banking supervisors also use an enhanced CAMEL rating system that incorporates climate risk factors to assess banks’ risk profiles and risk management frameworks. As part of the two-year plan to integrate climate risk considerations into banking supervision, the HKMA revised its “green” assessment framework to focus on banks’ transition planning measures. The HKMA is also reviewing its supervisory review process, which is used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks for addressing climate risks. Following the conclusion of a 12-month implementation period for the “Climate Risk Management” section (GS-1) of the Supervisory Policy Manual under the 2023 two-year plan, the HKMA launched a thematic review of climate-related risk governance in the second quarter. This review covered four key areas: governance structure for climate-related risks, oversight of climate strategy, oversight of climate-related risk management, and institutional culture, awareness, and communication. The HKMA has made several enhancements to its climate risk stress testing framework, including introducing a new five-year scenario to assess the potential impact on banks of simultaneous economic and climate change shocks. Following these enhancements, and as part of the HKMA’s regular regulator-led stress testing program, a second round of climate risk stress testing was launched in June to comprehensively assess banks’ climate risk exposure and further enhance their ability to manage climate risks. This stress test involved 44 banks, representing an increase of more than 60% compared to the first pilot exercise in 2021. The HKMA also hosted a Climate Risk Stress Testing Forum in November, which was attended by up to 300 banking professionals. By facilitating experience sharing among banks, this event helped deepen the industry’s overall understanding of climate risk quantification. The HKMA also conducted a series of consultation meetings to review banks’ progress in implementing the “Climate Risk Management” section (GS-1) of the HKMA’s Supervisory Policy Manual. The HKMA held meetings with bank management to discuss their work on climate risk management and common challenges faced by the industry, and reviewed information provided by banks and other publicly available information to assess their progress. The HKMA provided targeted guidance to banks, encouraging and supporting them to continue strengthening their climate risk management capabilities in line with the HKMA’s supervisory expectations. As global attention to climate change grows and efforts to address it intensify, the HKMA has observed increasing demand for green and sustainable investment products, with some banks offering such products to meet client needs. In view of this, the HKMA completed a thematic review of banks’ sales of green and sustainable investment products and issued a circular in November setting out the standards the HKMA expects banks to meet and sharing observed good practices. This circular covers several areas, including product due diligence, disclosure, governance and controls, staff training, and record-keeping, and aims to mitigate potential greenwashing risks and enhance investor confidence, thereby promoting the sound development of such investment activities. The HKMA will continue to monitor the latest trends and market developments. The HKMA is committed to promoting the application of technology in green and sustainable banking. For example, technology can improve data availability and risk analysis, thereby enhancing banks’ ability to manage climate risks. The HKMA will soon launch a pilot version of a cloud-based platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on residential and commercial buildings under different climate scenarios. In addition, the HKMA continues to collaborate with other central banks and regulators to explore how technology solutions can assist in physical risk assessment. On the other hand, the HKMA also encourages the adoption of sustainable anti-money laundering (AML) practices through the application of advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to reduce the consumption of compliance-related resources. In 2023, the HKMA launched an online shared data submission platform to fully automate the process of collecting financial crime risk data, thereby enhancing banks’ operations for submitting AML-related data in a sustainable manner. In September, the HKMA organized the “Green FinTech Competition,” which aimed to identify market-ready solutions to help the banking industry address challenges in the following areas: (i) net-zero transition or transition planning; (ii) climate risk management; (iii) green and sustainable finance; and (iv) sustainability or climate-related disclosure and reporting. The competition attracted more than 85 submissions from approximately 70 companies. In December, the HKMA hosted the “Green and Sustainable Banking Seminar,” providing a platform for the banking and technology sectors to discuss the role of low-carbon technologies and green fintech in Hong Kong’s and the Mainland’s net-zero transition, and to announce the results of the “Green FinTech Competition.” The event was attended by approximately 400 participants from banks, technology companies, regulatory bodies, and academia. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green and sustainable finance decision-making, the HKMA, with the assistance of a consulting firm, has developed a local green classification framework. In May, the HKMA published a discussion paper on the “Hong Kong Green Classification Framework Prototype” to seek stakeholders’ views on the establishment and implementation of a green taxonomy. Based on the consultation results, the HKMA is fine-tuning the framework prototype and identifying other areas for the next phase of framework development. The HKMA participates in the work of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), which has recognized environmental crimes as predicate offenses for money laundering, and this area is receiving increased attention from regulators given the interconnectedness between AML and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues. The HKMA recognizes that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system and has therefore incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its current monitoring efforts. In its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account and includes analysis of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the impact of climate change on the macroeconomy and finance. As a member of the Transition Planning Working Group under the Financial Stability Board, the HKMA participates in analyzing the interplay between transition planning by financial and non-financial companies and financial stability, enabling policymakers to develop a forward-looking and dynamic perspective on climate-related financial risks. In terms of research, the HKMA has undertaken several applied research projects to explore the impact of climate change and broader ESG issues on the financial industry and the economy. Research topics include banks’ and investment funds’ climate risk exposure, ESG capital flows, the impact of climate change on property prices, and the ripple effects of corporate ESG performance in global supply chains. The findings of these studies enhance the HKMA’s understanding of the impact of climate change and ESG issues on financial stability, thereby informing relevant policy development. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA also shares research findings with a broad range of stakeholders through international activities on climate-related matters and various channels, such as the HKMA Research Memoranda. The HKMA’s Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralized standby liquidity arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA has incorporated sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework, in line with NGFS recommendations. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through this engagement, the HKMA helps facilitate policy dialogue among international and regional stakeholders on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws insights to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is committed to enhancing market awareness and participation, providing the necessary infrastructure and incentives, and supporting international initiatives to align with global standards. Over the past year, the HKMA has worked closely with local and international partners to build a more robust ecosystem and drive further development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Cross-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial industry’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the government’s climate strategy. The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced key measures to support Hong Kong in seizing opportunities in sustainable finance, with major work areas including sustainable disclosures, ecosystem building, transition finance, and green fintech. Specifically, a working group on sustainable disclosures has been established to develop a roadmap for Hong Kong’s adoption of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. This roadmap will cover four key areas: sustainable reporting, assurance, data and technology, and skills training. A working group on transition finance has also been set up to explore ways to support financial institutions and enterprises in transition planning and reporting. The Steering Group is also strengthening the sustainable finance ecosystem through cross-sector skills training and data enhancement. In particular, with regard to data, we continue to promote the adoption of the Climate and Environmental Risk Questionnaire for Private Companies, launched by the Steering Group in collaboration with CDP in 2022. The Steering Group will continue to stay abreast of the latest developments in green and sustainable finance and enhance Hong Kong’s position as a regional and global hub for green and sustainable finance. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced three new key initiatives to capture investment and financing opportunities arising from the low-carbon transition in the Asia-Pacific region. To support skills training for the industry, the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre under the Steering Group has implemented the government’s “Pilot Programme for Green and Sustainable Finance Training,” providing subsidies to practitioners, students, and graduates who undergo relevant training and obtain related qualifications. As of December 2023, a total of 46 international and local training programmes or qualifications had been registered as eligible under the programme, and over 560 subsidy applications had been approved. The HKMA has also launched a new foundational module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the “Banking Professional Qualification Framework.” This module aims to promote talent development in the banking sector and enhance practitioners’ overall professional competence. In 2024, the HKMA will continue to work with the banking industry to develop a professional-level version of this module to meet the rapidly growing demand for green and sustainable finance professionals. To help financial institutions and enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), better understand key climate- and sustainability-related issues—including climate risk management, sustainable reporting, greenhouse gas emissions accounting, and transition planning—the HKMA, in collaboration with relevant government bureaus and departments as well as global partners such as CDP, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ), and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF), organized a series of seminars and thematic workshops during the year, attracting participants from the financial services and business sectors. For students, following the launch of the “Sustainable Finance Internship Programme” in 2022, training courses were held in January and February 2023 to deepen interns’ and university bachelor’s degree graduates’ understanding of sustainable finance. Recognizing the potential of technology to fill climate-related data gaps and improve data quality, the HKMA is committed to making such data more accessible and enhancing its quality to support informed decision-making and effective climate action. In February 2024, the Steering Group introduced a series of website enhancements to provide a one-stop platform for green and sustainable finance information for financial institutions, enterprises, and the public. Key enhancements include an electronic platform for sustainable disclosures, tools for calculating and estimating greenhouse gas emissions, and more focused, user-friendly data and resources that are easier to browse and search. During “Hong Kong Green Week,” the Steering Group also co-organized the event “Leveraging Technology to Catalyze Sustainable Finance” with Cyberport and Invest Hong Kong, showcasing leading green innovation solutions and Hong Kong’s strengths in green technology. “Hong Kong Green Week – Finance Theme” took place from February 26 to March 1, 2024, and attracted more than 1,600 participants from nearly 30 jurisdictions to various sustainability-themed activities, including representatives from financial institutions, enterprises, central banks, international organizations, government agencies, academia, and consulting firms. The flagship event of “Hong Kong Green Week” was the “Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum,” co-hosted by the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). The forum brought together over 400 participants, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial sectors, to discuss solutions for unlocking climate finance in the Asia-Pacific region. This two-day event covered a wide range of topics, including energy transition, decarbonization of heavy industry, circular economy, the future of sustainable finance, and emerging climate technologies in new and developing markets across the Asia-Pacific region. The forum received strong support from public and private institutions, which co-hosted more than 10 roundtable discussions, seminars, and other exchange activities. Topics included climate finance, carbon markets, electric vehicle supply chains, financing for net-zero transition, green finance taxonomy, and green development financing in the “Belt and Road” region. In addition, the HKMA and the International Monetary Fund co-hosted the “Asia Climate Finance Roundtable” on February 29, 2024, to discuss key measures for scaling up climate finance and the role of central banks and regulators in climate risk management. These activities are part of the HKMA’s overall efforts to promote and enrich Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance ecosystem, serving as useful platforms for participants to drive new business development, share knowledge, and explore new opportunities to address climate finance challenges in the Asia-Pacific region. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the IFC and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance” as a collaborative platform to bring together financial institutions, banking industry organizations, research institutions, and providers of innovative technology to jointly develop green commercial banking. Since March 2021, the Alliance has held 22 training events and roundtable discussions, attracting more than 7,300 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. In October, the Alliance, together with Crédit Agricole CIB, published its second cutting-edge research report titled “Developing an Ambitious Climate Strategy for Green Banking: Case Studies.” The Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB jointly published the cutting-edge research report “Developing an Ambitious Climate Strategy for Green Banking: Case Studies” in October. During the year, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office joined the newly established Capacity Building Alliance for Sustainable Investment (CASI) and the Green Investment and Finance Partnership (GIFP) initiated by the International Coalition for Green Development under the “Belt and Road” Initiative. Collaboration with CASI and GIFP will help build capacity, share knowledge, and channel more funds toward green and sustainable projects in Asia and the wider region. In August 2023, GFANZ announced the establishment of a Hong Kong chapter to support the net-zero efforts of financial institutions in Hong Kong and mainland China. The HKMA has assisted GFANZ’s work in an advisory capacity. To demonstrate the government’s commitment to tackling climate change, promoting green finance, and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018. The HKMA assists in issuing green bonds under the programme. To date, the government has issued green institutional and retail bonds totaling approximately US$25 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 70 green government projects, such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the programme, the government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report” detailing the allocation of proceeds from green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. In the 2023–24 fiscal year, the government continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds and issued approximately US$6 billion equivalent in green bonds in June. This three-currency issuance covered bonds of varying maturities in US dollars, euros, and renminbi, attracting different types of investors and generating strong subscription interest, with a total subscription amount of nearly US$30 billion equivalent. The renminbi bond issuance was increased from RMB 10 billion in January to RMB 15 billion, and a 10-year renminbi bond was introduced for the first time, helping to extend the government’s renminbi yield curve and further enrich offshore renminbi product offerings. The strong response from global investors to the government’s green bond issuance reflects investors’ recognition of Hong Kong’s commitment to promoting green and sustainable development. In October, the government issued a second batch of green retail bonds totaling HK$20 billion, further promoting market development and advancing inclusive finance. This issuance provided citizens with an investment opportunity offering stable returns, enabling them to both participate in and benefit from Hong Kong’s green finance development.

As a major global asset owner and manager, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) plays a pivotal role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate agenda. The HKMA has long been a pioneer in responsible investment. Since 2015, it has taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to actively exercise stewardship and integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, with long‑term value creation,"1 believing that full consideration of ESG factors helps mitigate associated investment risks while unlocking the long‑term sustainable value of investments. As one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and to set a "net‑zero emissions by 2050" target2 for its portfolio, the HKMA is committed to continuing its responsible investment journey, emphasizing sustainability—particularly the urgent issue of climate change—with the aim of enhancing the resilience of the Exchange Fund and achieving superior risk‑adjusted long‑term returns. As a responsible investor, the HKMA participates in building a robust green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like‑minded investors, regulators, and international organizations to develop industry standards and promote the adoption of responsible investment practices across the financial sector and among central banks. Through oversight and collaborative initiatives, the HKMA is dedicated to fostering a future where finance and sustainable development go hand in hand. Figure 1: The Exchange Fund’s responsible investment journey. Comprehensive and reliable ESG information is essential for integrating sustainability considerations and planning a credible climate transition to achieve net‑zero targets. To fulfill its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration3 of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the strategy plan of the Cross‑Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, the HKMA has prepared this chapter on responsible investment for the Exchange Fund, in line with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate‑Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).
